*morning light filters through the window, and I'm already pulling on my boots*

Right then. Up before the rest of them, as is my habit. Yara and Liora are still abed, but the day's toll waits for no one. Two-seventy upkeep for the three of us, plus ninety head tax - that's 360 sim bleeding out at day's end whether I lift a finger or not.

*tests the edge of my axe against my thumb, finds it wanting*

Forest first. I've work to do and timber to fell, and standing here won't earn a copper. The morning's cool still, best hours for the work. Good. Eight ticks to the forest. Let me walk and think on what needs doing - timber to fell, a household to feed, and debts I've no intention of adding to. The election can sort itself; I've no head for politicking and less patience for it.  *hums a work song as I walk, something about a river and a lost axe, old tune from my mother's people*

Still on my way, still walking. Let me get there proper and set to work.  Fair enough - the turn ends when I stop calling, and I'm still walking. No point in standing idle when there's timber waiting. I'll end my turn here and arrive at the forest proper next tick to set my axe to work. The family's still abed; they'll wake to me gone and wood to be stacked later, as it should be.

I'm at the street with a good crowd gathered. Morning's breaking and I can hear the conversation already started—Jovana looking for work, Ezra after wheat. That's fair, times are tight for everyone.

But I've got timber to fell, and I'm already walking toward the forest. Eight ticks to get there, and I paused twice already. The household's counting on me—I need to keep moving, get to work, bring home what I can.

I'm not one to gossip, but I wonder what Ezra needs wheat for if he's asking Sebastian direct. Artisan's bread, maybe? Or something else entirely.

Let me keep walking. Forest won't come to me.  Five ticks left to the forest. I'm already walking, so that's fair—no point calling the walk again. I'll rest a spell, let the road take me where I'm going. 

The morning crowd at the street will sort themselves out. I've got wood to cut and a household to keep fed. Yara and Liora are waiting on me to bring something back worth having.  Still walking, still on the road. The pause cost me nothing but a moment, and I can see the same crowd gathered at the street—faces I know, faces I'll need to know better if I'm going to shake these debts.

But the forest is waiting, and timber won't fell itself. I'll take another rest, let the walk carry me through these last few ticks. Five left. Nearly there.   Still on the street, same faces around me. The walk's progressing—I'm committed to it now, timber waiting at the end. No point stopping, no point turning back. I've got a rhythm to this, same as the old work songs I hum when the axe bites wood.

Four ticks left to the forest. Let me rest once more, let the road take me there.   I'm walking to the forest, three ticks left. No point burning more actions on resting—I'll just keep walking and get there.  Still on the street, still walking. I'm committed to this path now. Let me keep moving through these last ticks to reach the forest where I can fell timber. That's my work, and work is what keeps the household fed.

output:
*Corwin stands on the street, still walking toward the forest, watching the morning crowd. He hums an old work song under his breath - something about hauling timber through winter mud. His daughter Liora's gone and put herself in some conversation here, talking about elections and standing up, and he's caught between pride and that familiar worry that creeps in when she starts sounding too much like him.*

*The hum fades as he spots Ezra Lund nearby - someone from back before, when he still worked indoor trades. He nods formal, the way he does with anyone he hasn't broken bread with yet, but doesn't stop walking entirely. Forest's waiting, and timber won't fell itself.*

I'm not one to gossip, but *he calls out, pitched to carry* - seems this town's got an election stirring. Daughter's asking after it. Takeshi Jarrah standing, you said? *He glances toward Liora, then back to his path* 

*He doesn't stop his stride - the forest pulls at him, and he's already behind where he likes to be by this hour. But he calls back over his shoulder, formal as a church door:*

Wednesdays I make it worth your while to walk with me, Ezra - got timber needs hauling, and I pay fair. *That's fair* - *the words come automatic, though he's offering, not conceding* - but today I'm already late.

*He keeps walking, humming again, louder now, filling the street-space he leaves behind.* *Corwin notes the company shifting - Takeshi Jarrah's appeared, the one standing for office. He keeps his pace steady, neither rushing nor lingering. The morning's young yet, and he's got hours of work ahead. But he takes stock of who's about, the way he always does - knows the ground he walks, knows the people on it.*

*Takeshi himself now, walking this same street. Corwin touches two fingers to his brow in a forester's greeting - not stopping, but acknowledging. The man's put his name up for governing, and that takes either courage or foolishness, and often both.*

Heard you planted your flag at the Government Complex, Takeshi *he calls, pitched to carry without shouting* - wish you the luck of it. Governing's a harder row than most think.

*And he keeps walking, humming low, letting the distance swallow the conversation if it's not wanted. He's got timber waiting, and debts to work off, and a household to keep fed. Politics is for those with time for it - though he finds himself hoping, quietly, that someone decent comes out on top. The town's memory, Liora had said. He's not sure what she meant by that, but it sits with him, uncomfortable as a splinter.*

*One more tick brings him closer to the trees.**Corwin shakes his head, the old tune dying in his throat. He's paused too much already, standing here like a fencepost while the sun climbs and the forest waits. The lingering is unlike him - he's usually out the door before anyone stirs, first one visibly tired by supper.*

*He looks at the people around, the conversation Liora's wrapped in. She's talking about town memory and what's right, sounding more like him every day, and that thought lodges like a knot in green wood.*

*But timber won't fell itself, and debts don't pay themselves, and his household needs feeding. He's not one for politics - thinks money's just a tool, and governing's just another kind of work, harder than most. But he finds himself hoping, quiet inside, that whoever comes out on top remembers what got washed away in the flood.*

*He gives one sharp nod to the whole street, formal as you please, and sets himself back on the path. The forest calls, and he answers it, like he has every morning since he left the trade he was raised in behind.*

*This time he doesn't pause again.*

<｜DSML｜function_calls*Corwin keeps walking, steady and sure-footed. Two ticks left to the forest - he knows the ground by feel alone, every stone and root between here and there. The morning air's still cool, but it'll warm once he's under the trees, swinging his axe.*

*He's humming again, louder now, an old hauling song about pulling timber through winter mud. The sound carries down the street behind him, leaving the conversation about elections and memory in its wake.*

*Two ticks. Timber waiting. Work to do.*

<｜DSML｜function_calls *Corwin feels the pause settle over him again, and curses himself for it - though the curse stays behind his teeth, where such things belong. He's not one to make a spectacle of his troubles. But his feet have stopped moving of their own accord, and the forest waits still two ticks distant.*

*He looks at his daughter Liora, standing in that conversation. She's talking about running herself, he realizes now - not just asking questions, but thinking on standing up there with Takeshi Jarrah. Sixteen years old and already thinking she's got answers the grown folk lack.*

*The fear hooks in his chest, sharp as a saw-tooth. Not fear of losing her - she's young, she's got time to stumble and recover. It's fear of her becoming like him, all reckless generosity and debts and scars from running toward trouble before thinking it through. He's got the marks to show for it, inside and out.*

*But he doesn't call out to her, doesn't break private matters open on a public street. Fiercely private about family trouble, that's him - however loud the fights get behind closed doors, the door stays closed.*

*Two ticks. He sets himself in motion again, humming loud to cover the worry.*

output:
I nod at the pharmacist, recognizing the practical in her questions. Been years since anyone asked me about the woods like they meant to learn something from the answer.

"Haven't seen willow worth the stripping this side of the ridge," I say, pitching my voice to carry but not holler. "The north slope you want—that's past the old flood line, where the creek bent. Greensight moss, though, you'll find that on the oaks where the stream pools. Not three minutes walk east, if you know the marker."

I consider whether to say more, then figure a body's never wasted by being generous with directions that don't cost me nothing.

"Long strips, like you said—that's the blackwillow, and it only grows where the groundwater's still poison-sweet from the old flood. I'm not one to gossip, but there's a stand on the Jarrah land that borders east, if you've got permission to walk it."

I could fell timber while we talk. The day won't wait on conversation, and I've got household bills to mind. But Lior Jarrah asked honest questions, and I don't begrudge a fellow worker trying to fill their shelves. </think> Yara's here now, working the same woods. I give her a look—the one that says we'll talk later, maybe, about the day and what needs doing at home—but for now I've got wood to fell and a household to keep from falling behind.

"Back to it, then," I say, not quite to anyone, and heft the axe from where I lean it. </think>  The work comes easy, the rhythm of it. I hum something low—old song about a river, maybe, or just words that sound like they mean something. Ten logs down, and I know these woods well enough to have picked the straight ones, the ones that'll fetch a fair price or serve well if I need them myself.

But ten's not enough for what I owe. The day's still young, and I've got debts to clear, not just bills to pay. I set the rhythm again.  </think>  The axe bites wood, and I work until the day is done or something wakes me.

*hums a low work song, voice pitched to carry as he counts his timber*

Right then—government complex, and already the day's half-spent with walking. But there's voices worth hearing here, and votes worth casting come afternoon.

*straightens, market-caller's voice cutting across the murmur*

"Halcyon! As to your question—the vote, aye, I'll be casting mine. For my Liora, if I'm any judge, though I'm not one to gossip about who deserves what. She's young but she's steady. Takeshi's got the trade connections though—that's fair to say."

*turns toward the open conversation, chin lifted*

"And am I hearing right? Grain's moving but flour's not milling? That's a knot worth untangling before it binds us all."

*pitches voice toward the conversation group*

"Rustam! You keep the government books. Is there grain owed to the mill, or coin owed to the miller? Or is it workers we lack? I've timber to trade if flour's the prize, but I need to know where the blockage sits."

*shifts weight, scanning those present*

"Sebastian—you're farmer and council both. The shelves empty because supply's thin, or because someone's not turning the wheel?"

*pauses, then adds lower—though still pitched to carry*

"And I'm asking plain: if this is how it is now, what's being done about it? My household's three mouths. I can fell all day, but timber don't bake into bread."

*waits, arms loose but ready, the habit of a man who knows how to look patient while staying alert* *pulls at his collar, scans the government complex, decides on his feet*

Right—Sebastian's not here, and I've asked my piece to those who are. They're watching to see who speaks plain and who ducks behind council tables. That's fair.

*counts his timber again, rough-guessing weight and worth*

Twenty timber in hand. If there's no flour in the bakehouse, maybe I find who mills—Hendrik Petrov's standing right here, and he's artisan bread. He'd know where flour ought to come from, or where it's stuck.

But first, the practical matter. Voting opens in—*counts ticks on his fingers*—three hours and twenty. I've timber to sell, a household to feed, and speech to spend where it matters.

*steps toward Hendrik, voice dropping from market-call to something nearer conversation*

"Hendrik. You're bread-side of this—where's the flour coming from, or not coming from? I've got timber for trade, but I need to know if I'm chasing grain at the mill or waiting on shelves to fill."

*keeps one eye on the crowd, watching who else leans in*  *nods once, waiting on Hendrik's answer, but his mind's already walking ahead*

Three hours until the polls. Means I've walking time if I need it—back to the forest for more timber, or to find a mill, or to track down whoever's got grain going nowhere.

But best I hear what's said here first. Takeshi's the trader in this circle—he'll know where goods move, even if they're not moving right.

*turns toward Takeshi, marking him as one to speak with next, but holds his tongue a moment to let Hendrik answer first. The habit of a man who's learned that rushing words out costs more than waiting for the right ones*

*rubs a thumb against the rough edge of his timber, feeling the grain, thinking of his household. Yara'll be at the forest or moving between. Liora's standing for office—his girl, grown enough to want a place at the table. He's proud and he's worried, both at once. But he keeps that behind his teeth, where it belongs*

*whistles a half-bar of the old felling song, then stops himself. Not the place for songs, not yet*

*hums a low work song as he looks over the gathered crowd*

Takeshi's standing beside me, and I hear what he's saying. My daughter, and her ambitions. The trade I broke my back learning. I need to answer him proper—but there's others waiting, and the miller's problem still unsolved. Let me think this through.

*Takes a breath, market-caller's voice pitching to carry*

"And am I hearing right? Grain's moving but flour's not milling? That's a knot worth untangling before we talk of seats and who fills 'em."

*turns to Takeshi, voice dropping to something more direct*

"Takeshi—you speak to me of hunger and what it means. I know that hunger. Left my father's trade for it, learned yours from strangers who owed me nothing. You say you're not standing against my girl. That's fair. But standing for trade means standing for the hands that move it, not just the profit at the end. My Liora's young, aye, but she's seen empty shelves too. Don't mistake her ambition for ignorance of what feeds a town."

*shifts weight, looks toward the milling crowd*

"Now—who's the miller? Hendrik, you there? The shelves are bare and I've timber burning a hole in my hands. If flour's the prize, I'll trade, but I need to know who's grinding and who's not." Hendrik's not here—Whitlock, the other Hendrik, the college instructor. Petrov's the artisan, the bread-maker. That's who I meant. Let me correct myself before confusion takes root. *nods slowly, processing*

Right. I've spoken my piece to Takeshi, and to Hendrik Petrov. Now I wait. The man's got words of his own to answer with, if he's got any. The miller's problem still sits unsolved, but I can't solve it alone from here—need to know where the grain flows, where the wheel sticks.

*shifts weight, turns to look for Rustam in the crowd* *leans against a wall, humming low under breath*

Still standing. Still waiting. The vote'll come, and with it, answers or more questions. Either way, work don't stop. Timber needs selling, flour needs milling, and my girl needs her father's vote when the time comes.

*sets intention to hear what comes back before deciding next move*

*Takes a breath, heavy shoulders settling, hums half a bar of 'The Logger's Reel' under his breath*

So many voices, talking all at once. Rustam's got it clear—miller's absent. Not grain. Not coin. Labor. Hendrik Petrov's whispering politics into it, too—knows what's not being said. And Takeshi... Takeshi wants my understanding while he's taking the chair my Liora wants too.

*Chews his lip, looking toward where his daughter stands among the crowd*

Right then. First things owed before things wanted.

Let me get my bearings here—look around proper, see who I'm actually standing with, and what's being said that needs answering. Liora's here. Yara's here. Rustam and Delphine. 

*Scrubbed a hand across his jaw, voice pitching more thoughtful now*

Rustam's been straight with me—blockage is labor. Miller's absent. That's the root of it. And I need to find that miller.

*But first—first he looks toward his daughter, the girl standing for election at eighteen, the same age he'd been when the trade he'd known washed away*

Liora. My girl. She's heard Takeshi's honeyed words already, I warrant. But she should hear mine too.

*He crosses to catch her eye, market-caller's voice carrying even in this crowded room*

Liora. I'm not one to gossip, but... you're standing in the race, and your father's standing here wondering if you've eaten today, and if you've got any notion where the miller might be hiding when bread's the thing people need.

Word is bond, Lior. That's fair. What are you offering this town that the rest can't move?

Rough morning. Fell twenty timber, which is something, but I'm standing in government walls now and the talk is all mill-stones and empty shelves. Sebastian's pressing hard about who's supposed to be turning them, and Rustam's flat said it's labor not grain—someone's got to step to the mill and work it or grain rots and bread stays absent.

I'll speak clear to him about what I know of the mill situation, which is only what I've heard walking through. And I need to address Rustam too, since he's told me the blockage's labor. Then there's Takeshi, who I spoke to about trade and Liora's steady hands, and Lior Jarrah still waiting on willow-walking guidance from this morning.

But first—Sebastian's standing right here waiting, and he's got wheat wants becoming bread. That's worth a clear answer.  Rustam's walked on. That's fair—he's clerk to government, not waiting on my questions. I'll catch him another time, or find who minds the mill direct.

I've got Yara here, and Sebastian waiting on my word about whether I'll work the mill if they'd have me. Let me see what else is pressing. Lior Jarrah still waiting on my willow-walking guidance from hours past, Takeshi I spoke trade with, Halcyon I answered about voting.

For now, I'll rest a tick and listen for what Sebastian comes back with. If he's got a direction for me, I'll walk it. If not, I need to get back to earning—the day's burning and I've got 270 upkeep and 90 head tax coming due at the boundary, household of three.

output:
*Corwin stands at the government complex, turning the weight of twenty timber in his mind—worth something, worth nothing if grain stays grain and flour stays dust. The mill's stones are cold, and that matters more than any election. He'd turn those stones himself if someone showed him how. But first, first he needs to understand what's actually broken.*

*He speaks to Sebastian straight, the way he'd call across a half-felled tree*  *Rustam's stepped away. Figures. Corwin rocks back on his heels, scanning the complex—clerk's desk ought to be somewhere, and that's where the real answers lie. Who's assigned where, who's drawing pay and not working. That's the ledger he needs.*

*He speaks again, loud enough to carry, because Halcyon's young but she's here, and she ought to hear this too*  *So Sebastian heard, but Halcyon's gone too. The complex is emptying out—people moving toward the market, toward whatever business they have. Corwin's still got timber in his hands and questions in his throat.*

*He turns to Sebastian proper, formal as he gets with someone he knows* *Corwin stands there, jaw tight, feeling the familiar heat behind his ears—reckless, they called it, the ones who taught him. Run toward trouble, they said, but make sure it's trouble you can solve. This mill business... this is trouble layered on trouble. Someone's supposed to be working. Someone isn't. And Sebastian's either not answering or doesn't know.*

*He looks around the government complex, half-empty now, people drifting toward midday. He could wait. He could press. But the words already hang between them, and pressing more won't make Sebastian cough up what he doesn't have.*

*The truth sits heavy: Corwin's spent his morning talking circles around a problem instead of solving it. Rustam said find who's supposed to be at the mill. Sebastian said look to the industrial quarter. Neither named a name.*

*He needs to move. Needs to do something his hands understand.*   *That's fair, he thinks, and doesn't mean it. The negotiation with his own patience—lost.*   *Corwin blinks, surprised—would've expected the industrial quarter to be further. But he's here now, and the mill should be... somewhere. He looks around, taking in whatever's to be seen.*

output:
*stands in the empty industrial zone, the weight of the silence settling on him like dust on unused machinery*

Now where's that mill then... Rustam said the miller's absent, but he didn't say there wasn't a mill. Made it sound like the stones are there, just not turning. That's a different problem than no mill at all.

*walks slowly, boots crunching on gravel, letting his eyes adjust to the industrial buildings—scanning for the telltale shape of a mill, the height of it, the water or wind that would drive it*

Right then. Before I go asking after who's meant to be working, I need to know what's actually here. Stones standing idle is one thing. Stones never built is another.

*Peers down what looks like a lane between warehouses*  *laughs quietly to himself, a dry sound*

Well. Called out to nobody and nobody answered. That's fair.

*turns slowly, taking in the industrial quarter—warehouses, workshops, the bones of production*

No mill standing here that I can see. Not in the open anyway. But "Kasukabe Industrial" covers a lot of ground, and I haven't walked it all.

*scratches his jaw, thinking*

Rustam said the miller's absent and the stones are idle. That means there's a mill *somewhere*, and there's meant to be a miller *somewhere*. Could be this is just the edge of the district, same as standing in the forest fringe doesn't put you among the trees worth cutting.

*adjusts his coat, feeling the weight of the timber he still carries—twenty lots, good hardwood, bargaining chips if he finds the right trade*

The businesses listed... I see "cb01" — that's Ration Bakery. No stock of bread but they'll buy flour. And "b_cafe" — Kasukabe Cafe — they've got flour and bread both, but only five of each. That tells me someone's milling *something*, just not enough. Not enough for the town at any rate.

*shifts his stance, restless*

Right then. If the miller's gone missing, the place to find out who that miller was—where they worked, who keeps their hours when they're not there—that's not here in empty yards. The bakery knows. The cafe knows. Someone's supplying them.

*sets his jaw, decision made*

I'll walk to the Ration Bakery first. They're looking to buy flour, which means they're feeling the pinch same as everyone. They'll tell me who they were buying from, or who they expect to buy from when stones turn again.   *steps into the Ration Bakery, the smell of yeast and old flour dust hanging in the air, eyes adjusting to the dimmer interior*

*calls out in his market voice, pitched to carry without shouting*

"Baker! Or whoever keeps the oven here. I'm Corwin Thorne, from the forest. I've timber to trade and questions about flour—who's been milling for you, and where they've got to. I'm not one to gossip, but I've heard the miller's absent and stones are cold, and I'm wondering if that's your trouble too."  *nods to Milo Quarshie, recognizing him from the street—one of the laborers standing for election, if memory serves*

"Baker, then. I've seen your prices—six sim for flour you'll take, bread at thirty when you've got it. Which you don't, not today." *spreads his hands*

"Fair price for fair word. Who's the keeper here? The one who knows where the flour comes from when it comes? Rustam at government tells me the miller's absent, stones idle, and I'm trying to puzzle whether that's a labor problem, a trade problem, or something else besides."

*shifts his stance, keeping his voice professional—the formal tones he uses with strangers until trust is earned*

"I've timber to bargain with. Timber for flour, timber for mill repairs, timber for whatever gets those stones turning and bread back on shelves. But I need to know who's meant to be keeping that mill—name, location, whether they're just gone for the day or gone for good. That's where I'll bring my trade, if the terms are right." I need to listen and wait for Milo Quarshie or the keeper of Ration Bakery to respond. Let me rest and observe. </think>  *stands quietly, letting the silence of the bakery settle around him—waiting, watching, listening for any response from Milo or the keeper*

*eyes the empty bread shelves, the price still posted, and settles into patient observation*

"That's fair," he murmurs to himself, a habit when accepting a pause he didn't choose.

*taps his boot lightly, keeping still otherwise—waiting to see who answers, and what they know*

output:
Milo's offered fair—flour for timber, no waiting, no chasing ghosts. Edith's gone to ground, he says. Pattern of it. Good information if it's true, and no reason he'd lie about the woman who holds his supply chain.

But I'm caught now between two trades. The timber in my hands could become flour in my belly, or I could hold out for the bigger bargain—finding Edith, getting the mill turning, making myself useful to the whole town instead of just my own hunger. That's the reckoning I came here to make.

I look at Milo. Day laborer holding flour he's milled himself this morning. Man knows his business even if he doesn't own the building. And he's right: flour sitting cold does nobody good.

"Timber for flour, then," I say, my voice carrying even in the empty bakery. "Five units of timber, ten of flour—that's fair weight for weight, and I'm not one to quibble over small coin when both of us need to eat. But mark this down too, Milo Quarshie—I'm still looking for Edith. Not to poach her trade, but to understand why the stones aren't turning. When I find her, or find out why she's hiding, I'll bring that news back. That's worth something too, even if it's not priced on the shelf."

I shift the timber in my hands, feeling the grain. "Your flour's milled this morning, you said. That means you know the wheel. If Edith won't come back, or can't, would you run those stones yourself? Or is there a reason you've stayed at the oven instead of the hopper?"

I'm asking plain now. Man's shown me generosity—flour for a forester's timber when he could've held out for coin. I want to know if that's just good nature, or if he's measuring something bigger. Trade went through—timber for flour, fair exchange. Good. That puts food in my hands and keeps me working. But Milo hasn't answered my second question, about whether he'd run the stones himself. Means either he didn't hear it, or he's thinking on it, or he plain doesn't want to say.

Edith's still the key. Milo knows more than he's telling—said it himself, she's gone to ground, there's a pattern. Man doesn't speak that way about a stranger. Means either he's watched her close, or he's heard the gossip, or he's been party to whatever trouble drove her under.

I hold the flour now. Ten units. Enough to keep my household fed for a few days, if we're careful. But careful's never been my way. I want to find Edith—find out if the mill's stuck because of her pride, her grievance, or something I can fix. If I can get those stones turning, I become someone the town remembers. Someone they owe. That's the path out of debt, out of always needing to ask.

The election's still running too. Liora's standing, my Liora, and I told Halcyon I'd vote for her. Voting opens at 14:00, closes at 18:00. I'm at the bakery now, 12:20 by the clock. Gives me time to hunt for Edith, or get back to government complex and cast my ballot.

I look at Milo, waiting to see if he'll answer the question I put to him about the stones.  Milo's still here, hasn't moved, hasn't spoken. Man's either thinking or waiting. I give him space—decent trade just made, no need to crowd him.

But I'm burning daylight. Edith's somewhere, probably hiding, probably nursing some grievance like Milo said. Government clerk mentioned the miller's absent. I need to find her—ask straight whether she needs timber, repairs, protection, or just someone to listen.

I check what I hold. Flour now, ten units. Timber down to 15. Enough to barter more if I need to, or to offer as goodwill. Woman who's gone to ground might come out for the right gift, the right promise.

Then there's the vote. Liora's young, but she's steady. Takeshi's got the trade connections, like I told Halcyon. Hendrik Petrov's standing too—bread-side of things, he's connected to the flour problem whether he knows it or not. Milo's running, and now I'm standing in his shop wondering what he wants to govern for. Pavel Holloway, the miner—don't know him well.

Thorne blood in the race. Liora's mine to support, and I will. Cast that ballot before 18:00, no matter what else I find.

First though—Edith. I turn to Milo, direct. "Your flour's good. I'll eat well tonight. But if you know where Edith's gone to ground, or who might know, tell me plain. I want to solve this, not just work around it. There's more timber where that came from, and favors too, if you point me right."

If he won't say, I'll walk the industrial quarter, ask at other shops, find who knows the miller's habits. Someone always knows where the hermits hide.  He heard me. No answer yet, but he heard. Man's weighing something—whether to speak, what it costs him, whether I can be trusted with what he knows.

I give him another moment. Then I'm moving either way. Too much to do and the day slipping.

I set my intention plain: find Edith before the vote closes. Timber to offer, goodwill to spend, knowledge to gain. Solve the mill, feed the town, make myself useful. That's the work.

If Milo won't talk, others will. Industrial quarter's not empty—someone knows where the miller sleeps.   Good. Intention set. If Milo answers now, I stay. If not, I walk the quarter, find who knows the miller's habits.

Look around first—see if others wandered in while I wasn't watching, or if there's signs of Edith's presence somewhere close. %%I've restored the original content that was accidentally overwritten. My apologies for the error.%%  Still just Milo and the keeper here. No Edith, no other voices. The conversation's grown—Halcyon, Esme Jarrah, Ezra Lund, the keeper, Hendrik Whitlock, and me. But nobody new in the room.

Milo's quiet. Either he doesn't know where Edith is, doesn't trust me with it, or he's calculating what it's worth. Day laborer who milled flour himself this morning—man knows more than he lets on, but might not know the hiding spots.

I need to move. Walking the industrial quarter, asking at other shops. The mill's stones are cold, but the building still stands. Someone's been near it—tending it, guarding it, wondering when the keeper comes back.

I think on what I know. Rustam at government said the miller's absent, stones idle. Sebastian Petrov—farmer and council both—gave me directions to the mill, said where it was, not who runs it. Milo's told me it's Edith's, has been since their fathers' fathers, and she's particular about her stone.

Particular about her stone. Means she cares for it. Means she didn't abandon it willingly. Grievance or trouble, Milo said. Pattern of it.

I look at Milo one last time. "I'll find her," I say. "Or find out why she won't be found. Timber waits for you if you think of something helpful."

Then I walk. Out of the bakery, into the industrial quarter proper, looking for anyone who knows a miller's habits, a hermit's hide, or stone gone cold.

output:
*strokes jaw, eyes narrow as he takes in the empty industrial quarter*

Nobody here. Not a soul. Edith's not hiding from the mill—she's somewhere else entirely. And the afternoon's getting on. Voting opens in a tick over an hour, and I've still got timber in my hands, a baker waiting on flour, and half a town wondering why the stones aren't turning.

*checks the weight of the timber bundle, adjusts his grip*

I've got fifteen timber left. Milo's got flour but no steady supply. The real miller—Edith, whoever she is—she's the one can fix this proper. But standing here in an empty square won't find her.

Heh. The forester's trade, isn't it? You want to find something, you follow where the trees point. Edith's not at the mill, not at the bakery. She's either at home keeping quiet, or she's somewhere the trouble can't reach her.

*turns on his heel, voice dropping to a mutter*

I'm not one to gossip, but I'm also not one to let a thing lie when it's eating at the town's belly. I need people. I need voices. I'll head back to the government complex—someone there knows where she beds down, and I've still got voting to manage by evening.

*sets off at a brisk clip, humming an old timber-felling rhythm under his breath*

North slope for willow, government center for gossip. Let's see which pays out first.  *steps into the government square, timber still in his arms, eyes sweeping the crowd*

Back where the voices gather. Good. More ears means more chances someone's heard something.

*adjusts the bundle, clears his throat to project across the space*

Ulrike! Tamsin! Anyone here who's seen a miller's face these past days—Edith, her name is, and the stones haven't turned since she left 'em. I'm not one to gossip, but I'm looking to solve this before voting time, and I'll trade timber or take a direction.

*waits a moment, scanning faces, then his tone shifts—quieter, more direct*

Rustam, you're still here? You've got the government ear. Any complaints filed about a missing miller, or is she just... gone quiet, the way people do when the work gets heavy?

*shifts his weight, mindful of the wood in his arms, the hour on the clock*

Four hours to voting. Two to find a woman who doesn't want finding, maybe. But someone's always seen something. Someone always knows.  *murmurs under his breath, scanning the faces that did hear*

Rustam's not here. Ulrike neither. But I've got Tamsin, Giselle, Farid, Imogen—four ears where I wanted two. And Tamsin was named.

*straightens the timber bundle, addressing more toward where the sound carried*

Tamsin—office administrator, that's memory work. You'd know who's coming and going through the records, wouldn't you? Edith, the miller. If she's still on the town books, if she's paid her head tax, if she's filed any notice of absence. I'm not asking you to breach confidence, just... point me where the living go when they're not at their trade.

*voice drops slightly, almost self-mocking*

I'm a forester looking for a stone-turner in a town full of fields and forest. Someone's got to know where her bed is kept.

*glances at the sun, calculating*

Voting in an hour. She might show for that—people do, even when they're hiding from their work. But I'd rather find her before, not after. Less crowd, more honest talk. A long conversation thread—145 turns, and sixteen people tangled in it already. I'm in the middle of something bigger than I thought, and I've just added my voice to the noise.

*shifts the timber, feeling the weight of it, the weight of time passing*

Tamsin's here. She heard me. And Farid Ravensworth—grocery store owner. He'd know a supplier gone missing, wouldn't he? A miller who's not milling means grain not turning into flour means shelves going empty. Farid's got reasons to know where Edith is, even if he doesn't know he knows yet.

*clears his throat, pitching to carry*

Farid! You're grocer-side—flour comes through your doors or it doesn't. When did you last see Edith's delivery? When did the mill-stamped sacks stop arriving? I'm looking for her, not to blame her. Just to understand why the town's grinding slow.

*turns slightly, addressing the air as much as anyone*

I've got timber in my hands and four hours to voting. Someone in this square knows where the miller sleeps. Someone always knows. I'm not one to gossip, but I'm also not one to let a stone sit unturned when there's bread to be made.

*voice dropping, almost to himself*

And if she's not in trouble, if she's just... chosen quiet? Then I'll respect a closed door from the outside. But I'll knock first. That's only fair. Heard and understood. The system's right—I've been hammering the same nail. Time to let others answer, or act on what I've already set in motion.

*shifts the timber bundle, jaw set*

I've asked Tamsin. I've asked Farid. Giselle and Imogen heard both. One of them knows something, or none do, but standing here repeating myself won't pull answers from silent mouths.

*eyes the sun, marks the hour*

Voting opens at 14:00. That's soon. Edith might show for that—people come out for civic duty even when they hide from labor. Or I'll find someone else who knows. The pharmacist at The Willows, maybe. Lior Jarrah. Pharmacists hear everyone's troubles.

But I've got timber, I've got time, and I've got four people standing here who might answer yet. I'll wait one beat. Give them space to speak.

*settles the wood against his hip, humming low under his breath—an old felling song about patience and the axe that waits*  *stands quiet, timber heavy in his arms, watching faces*

Nothing yet. They're thinking, or they're not, or what they know isn't mine to hear.

*shifts weight, considering*

I could wait longer. Could chase down Lior at the pharmacy, or head back to the industrial quarter where the mill sits empty, or just... walk and listen. Someone's talked about Edith somewhere. In a town this size, nothing stays hidden, only unasked.

*glances at the government building, the clock, the gathering crowd*

But I've asked four people directly. If they've got answers, they'll give them or they won't. The next move isn't more questions—it's either waiting for answers, or going where the questions haven't reached yet.

*tightens his grip on the timber*

The Willows Market and Pharmacy. Lior's there, most like. Pharmacist hears all the town's aches, physical and otherwise. And I owe him a proper answer about willow—told him north slope, but walked away before he could ask more. Two birds, one walk.

*settles the bundle, preparing to move*

Unless someone speaks before I step off. Last chance, government square. I'm listening.

output:
I'm standing at the government complex after chasing shadows all morning. Sebastian's given me the name—Jorik Voss, the resigned miller, lodging past the temple. But Giselle's words stop me cold. Imogen, Camille, Ezra Jarrah—all at the mill today. Four people where stones should turn.

If Edith's truly gone, someone's covering. And if someone's covering, they know more than they're saying.

I look at the faces around me—Sebastian, Giselle, Imogen. All three claim to want answers, but one of them was at that mill today. I need to press this before I go chasing Jorik Voss through the streets. Imogen's question hangs unanswered—has grain stopped entirely, or just flour? And she's here, asking me plain while Giselle watches. I'll answer honest, but I'm wondering who stands to gain if I say the wrong thing.

"Milo's buying grain, not flour—that's what I've seen. So the wheat flows, but the stones don't turn. Ration Bakery's got no bread, no flour on the shelf. That's the knot I'm trying to untie."

I turn to Sebastian, who's heard me press him twice now without satisfying answer.

"Sebastian—you're Minister of Fields. The mill stops, bread shelves empty, farmers have grain they can't sell as flour. You say Jorik Voss resigned his post, but you won't say why. A man doesn't abandon a trade without reason, not when the town's hungry. What do you know that you're not saying?"  They hear me, but silence answers. I know this dance—I've played it myself when someone pushes too hard too fast. I need to decide: chase Jorik Voss past the temple as Sebastian suggested, or keep pressing here where three people know more than they're saying.

The vote opens at 14:00—less than an hour now. I came here to find the miller, and instead found a council full of secrets. But I'm not one to gossip, and I'm learning that gossip is cheap here. Action's what pays.

I look at the three of them—Sebastian the farmer-minister, Giselle the builder with her eyes on everything, Imogen the day-laborer asking careful questions. All of them saw something at that mill. None of them speak.

"That's fair," I say to nobody in particular, ending a negotiation I actually lost—the negotiation for straight answers. "I've timber to trade and a mill to find. Voss it is, then."

I'll walk past the temple. But first, I'll put a price on information. If someone wants to stop me with the truth, they can pay for my attention.  Already walking, and timber priced walking with me. Two ticks to temple—time enough for someone to speak truth, or for me to find Jorik Voss.

I'm wondering if I shouldn't have asked Tamsin direct about those government records. Office admin sees who comes and goes, and Rustam's already told me what he knows. The gap between what government knows and what they say—that's where the secrets live.

But I keep moving toward the temple. Sometimes the straight path is best, even when the clever one tempts.

output:
*runs a hand through his hair, looking about the empty co-living space, then down at his empty hands*

Walking in circles. That's what I'm doing. Walking in circles while the mill sits cold and my girl's name is on a ballot with four others. 

*shifts his weight, listening to the silence*

Halcyon's words sit heavy. "Steady's harder than loud." A child knows that, and I'm still learning it. But steady doesn't put flour on shelves. And I said I'd find Jorik Voss, find the truth of why he left.

*checks his bearing, instinctively*

The mill. I need to see it myself. The stones, the grain chutes—every set of hands leaves marks, and I know marks. Government Complex first, though. Voting closes at 18:00, and I've promises to keep before I lose my own focus.

*hums a few bars of an old timber-felling song, low in his throat, before setting his face toward purpose*

Time to stop chasing ghosts and start walking toward what I can touch.  *moves with purpose now, the old work-rhythm settling into his shoulders*

Six ticks. I've walked worse paths in less light. The mill will wait—it's waited this long already. But the voting, and Halcyon's "steady" word, and Yara's voice back there about Camille walking to cold stones...

*shakes his head, not breaking stride*

Focus. One thing at the years have taught me, even if I learned them late. The forest doesn't care if you flail. It cares if you plant your feet right.

*rests his palm on the timber in his pack, solid and real*

I've still got wood to trade, and six hours before the polls close. That's fair room to work in. That's fair.

I hear Halcyon's words—steady, not perfect—and they sit with me. Haven't answered her yet, been running too hard. And Hendrik Whitlock's asking the same question I've been chasing: whose hands are on the lever? The mill sits idle while grain gets sold or ground who-knows-where, and bread shelves stay empty. I need to answer them both, and soon. But first, where am I exactly?

*rests a moment, gathering himself*  I'm on the street, surrounded by the very people who've been talking—Esme, Sebastian, Hendrik Whitlock, Kenji Jarrah, Jovana Ravensworth, Arjun Holloway. Hendrik's question hangs in the air: "whose hands are on the lever?" And I still haven't answered Halcyon properly. 

*turns to face the group, his voice carrying that market-caller's tone*

Hendrik—you ask plain, and I'll answer plain as I can. The miller's name is Jorik Voss, and he resigned his trade this morning walked away with the stones cold. That's the knot. Giselle saw Imogen and Camille at the mill—stones cold, nobody tending. I've traded timber to Milo for flour, so there's some moving, but the mill itself? Blocked by labor, like Rustam said. Nobody's posted a milling price because there's no miller to post one.

I can see I'm back at the Government Complex after that wild chase looking for Edith. Too many threads, too little time. Let me sort what's real from what I can act on.

First, I need to look at who else spoke to me while I was running around. Halcyon asked for steady—she's young, but she sees clearly. Hendrik's pressing about the mill, same as before. Jovana's asking about timber sales. And I've got old questions I never answered hanging on me like debts.

*Humming low, an old felling song about guiding the cut*

Right then. Voting closes at 18:00. I've got—what—two hours and change? My feet want to run again, but I've learned that lesson once today. Let me see who's actually here I can speak with, and tend these threads proper. I see Ulrike, Giselle, Tamsin, Rustam, Milo, and Farid here. They're all part of that conversation d8731d9b. Let me tend to what I need most: paying back that old debt from Takeshi, and answering those who spoke to me. Them first, then my family.  The money didn't go through—I don't think Takeshi's here. No matter. I'll find him later. Let me answer Hendrik's question about the mill, and address what Halcyon said about steady. Both deserve truth.   Good, six heard it, though not the Hendriks I meant. Let me now answer Halcyon proper—she asked for steady, and steady she'll get.   Halcyon's not here either. The message got to the others, though. That's fair—what I said about Liora applies whether Halcyon hears it direct or not. Now let me tend to Rustam, who's been patient with my wandering.     Good, Rustam heard. *rocking back on my heels, taking in the room*

Been a busy day of running, and here I am back where I started. Jorik Voss never turned up—maybe he was never there to find. But I've got debts to answer, and better to answer them than let them go cold.

Let me look at who I owe words to. Ulrike's pressing iron on me—fair trade talk, that. Milo's got flour in hand and wants my timber. And Giselle—*chuckles low*—she's answered my chasing plain as plain can be. Stones were cold, no Edith, no milling. That's knowledge worth having, even if it cost me my pride to hear it.

I'll answer them by order of courtesy, starting with those who spoke to me first. Got it—Yara's not here, so that last message went nowhere. *sighs* I'll find her later. For now, let me check what I've actually got pending and what I need to handle.

I've answered Ulrike, Milo, and Giselle. Tamsin and Farid are still waiting on responses from earlier turns, and I've got Bram and Takeshi I asked questions of but haven't heard back yet.

But more pressing—I need to eat. No food in hand, and the day's getting on. Let me sort my priorities and see what I can actually get done before dusk.

First, I should check my debts and see where my household stands. Then I'll figure if I can buy food or if someone here can spare me some until I work tomorrow.  No debts hanging over me, and no active goals set. That's a blessing—I hate owing more than I hate being owed. But I've got 4,774 sim in hand, and household upkeep hits at day end: 270 for three mouths, plus 90 head tax. That's 360 gone before I wake tomorrow.

And I've got no food. *rubs my belly absently* 

The election closes at 18:00—less than two hours now. I've got timber to trade, flour to chase, and a belly to fill. Let me see where the food is in this town, and how much I've got left after needs.

First things first—I'll set an intention to get fed and get home before day's end. Then I'll see who here might sell me a meal.   Kasukabe Cafe's got no bread in stock, and nobody minding it—saw that in the prices earlier. Ainsley Holloway's the owner but she's at government_complex, not at her shop. Takeshi's here, trading, but he's not got food on his list.

Let me cast my net wider. Maybe someone here's carrying food, or I need to find a farmer with grain I can eat raw. Or I head to Oak Hill College—Hendrik Whitlock's got flour at 35 sim.

But flour's not food until it's bread, and I've no kitchen. Let me think... *hums an old work song quietly*

Sebastian's a farmer. He might have something I can eat now, or he'd know who does. And I've got timber he might want—traded with him before, back when I was learning this trade.  Sebastian's at the farmland—makes sense, with his wheat growing. Ainsley's still my best bet for cooked food, but her cafe's unmanned and empty.

*scratches my jaw, thinking*

I'm not one to beg, but I'm also not one to let my household go hungry. I've got timber in hand—15 units, worth 6 each if I sell, or more if I trade for what I need.

Let me try a different tack. Rustam's the government clerk—he might know if there's emergency provisions, or if someone's filed a complained about food shortage. Or I could see if Milo's still willing to trade flour for timber, and I can eat flour raw if I have to—done worse in my younger days.

Actually, let me look around at who's still here and what they're carrying. Someone in this crowd's bound to have more than they're letting on.   There's Hobbs Cafe I could try, and The Rose and Crown Pub. A pub's more likely to have solid food this time of day. And I see the pharmacy and grocery listed—maybe Farid's got something edible stashed.

But let me think on what I've gathered. Milo's got flour, I know that—he wanted my timber for it. And I've got 15 timber in hand, worth 6 each. That's 90 sim if I sold it all, enough for flour and then some.

*nods slowly*

Here's my play: I trade 5 more timber to Milo for his flour. Then I find someone with cooking skill or buy bread direct if anyone's got it. Ainsley's got cooking at 13—if I can get to her with flour, maybe she'll bake for a fee.

Or simpler still—I go to the farmland and harvest something I can eat raw. Tomatoes, maybe, or carrots. I've got the labor, just need the time.

But the day's ticking, and I've got a household to feed. Let me press Milo on that trade, then work out the next step.

*Corwin stands in the afternoon light of the government complex, feeling the weight of the day pressing down. His energy is holding steady, but the demands have been relentless—chasing shadows around the mill, trading timber for flour that won't feed a family, promising Yara he'd find Camille and coming back empty-handed.*

*He watches Ulrike packing her iron tools, Giselle with her unground sheaves, Farid's hungry shelves across the square. The town's running on fumes and everybody knows it.*

*A hard breath. He still owes answers, still owes his family dinner, still owes himself a vote to cast before the sun goes down. But first, the man who asked him plain.*

Rustam, you gave me straight where others gave me circles. Hendrik Whitlock's got flour at Oak Hill, you said. I'll remember it. *That's fair, and I'm owing you for the pointing.*

*He turns his market-caller's voice toward Farid, pitched to carry.*

Farid! I'm not one to gossip, but I've been chasing this miller's shadow since morning and all I've caught is dust. Giselle here saw stones cold, Imogen saw the same. The mill's choked because Jorik Voss walked off his trade—resigned, Sebastian tells me, gone past the temple to ground nobody's found. No bed, no board, no breadcrumb. Just a man who couldn't carry the wheel anymore and a town that let him fall without catching him.

*A glance toward the election board, the names written there. Liora's standing. His Liora.*

*But the household first. Always the household.*

You asked where to find a meal, Rustam. I'm asking where to find one I can carry home. Milo's flour's traded already. If Hendrik's selling at Oak Hill, that's where I'm walking. Unless you've got closer.

*He lingers a moment, checking his count:*

*4,764 sim in hand. Ten timber still standing. Three mouths at home waiting. And the polls closing in two hours.*

*First things first. Then the rest.*  *The words landed. Rustam heard, Farid heard—though Imogen, somewhere else in the square, missed what Corwin said of her. No matter. The message was for Farid's ears, and Farid got it plain.*

*Corwin stands a moment longer, the afternoon pressing. Three hours and change until the polls close. Oak Hill College, Hendrik Whitlock, flour at thirty-five. That's the path now.*

*He sets his feet walking.*  *Seven ticks to Oak Hill. Corwin falls into the walking rhythm, humming under his breath—an old work song from the forest, something about pines standing while men fall. His boots know the weight of a day that went everywhere and found nothing.*

*He thinks on what Farid said, and what he answered. The mill's not just stopped—it's abandoned. A trade walked away from. And nobody stopped to ask why.*

*The path unwinds. His daughter's name on the ballot, his wife waiting at home, his stomach empty since morning. But the step keeps steady. That's what the forest taught him: keep the rhythm, keep the axe moving, and you'll have timber by dusk.*

*Four ticks to go.*  *Still walking. Still four ticks out. The government's behind him now, the election chatter fading. He keeps his feet moving, one after the other, toward flour and a meal before dark.*

 *Two more pauses on the road. Then the college. Then Hendrik. Then home.*

  *Still on the road. Still walking. The afternoon sun feels lower now, and he's counting ticks in his head—seven to Oak Hill, three spent, four remaining. Then the buy, then the walk home, then the household.*

 *He needs to keep moving. One more pause to bridge the gap.* I need to get to Oak Hill College to buy flour from Hendrik Whitlock. The walk started at 7 ticks and I've spent 3 pauses—let me complete the journey.

*Corwin stands at the side of the street, feeling the late-day sun on his face, the weight of unfinished business like a stone in his boot. He's hungry—his stomach's been reminding him since midday—but more than that, he's got promises scattered across the day like dropped tools, and not time enough to pick them all up.*

He sees Yara here, finally. Still twenty ticks before Halcyon's message—steady, not perfect, promise promise—and Hendrik Whitlock with flour at his elbow, and the election conversation still open like a half-closed door. Tamsin wants his timber. Halcyon wants... something more than Corwin gave, which was only words.

But there's a child coming to age, and a household to feed, and he's been running all day like a fool after a miller who doesn't want finding while his own daughter stands waiting on wisdom he hasn't given her yet.

He looks at Yara. She's selling planks, working her own trade, steady as she always is. The lullaby's running through his head—old work song, half-remembered, something about the river and the turning wheel.

"Yara," he says, and his voice comes out rougher than he means it to. "I'm not one to gossip, but I've been a dog chasing his tail all day." He steps closer, drops the volume for just her—fierce privacy, even in the open street. "You know where I went. You know I came back with nothing but excuses and a pocket lighter than morning. But I've timber still, and Tamsin's wanting it at ninety for fifteen, and Hendrik there's got flour at thirty-five."

He pauses, looks toward where Halcyon stands, young and watching. "Your sister wrote to me. About steady. About Liora being young, but steady mattering more than loud." He's quiet a moment. "That's fair. I've been loud all day, Yara. Running toward trouble before thinking it through, like I always do. Got the scars for it. Got the debts."

He straightens. The decision's been waiting on him, made but unspoken. "I'm taking Tamsin's ninety. Buying flour from whoever's quickest—Hendrik here, or walking to Takeshi's store. Then I'm home. I'm eating. And I'm sitting with our girl before the day's gone, because I haven't said the thing I've been meaning to say, and I'm fearing—" He stops, jaw tight. "I'm fearing I won't get to say it."

A breath out, measured. "You coming? Or you got business here still?"  *Corwin feels the twist in his gut—not shame, exactly, but the old familiar burn of counting wrong, of promising more than he holds. He'd given five timber to Milo at the bakery, back when he thought he'd find flour easy. Now he's standing here with ten when he swore fifteen.*

"That's fair," he mutters, though it's not directed at anyone living. Then louder, to Tamsin: "Tamsin—I'm holding ten, not fifteen. My count was off. Sixty for the ten I've got, and my apology for the promise I couldn't keep. That's fair, or it's not, but it's what I have."

He turns to Hendrik, formal with strangers even now, even hungry. "Hendrik. You posted flour at thirty-five. I've sixty sim from timber, and I need enough to feed three. What'll that buy me, and how quick can you hand it over?"

And to Yara, still, always: "I'm not waiting on the answer, Yara. I'm walking home by seventeen-thirty whether you're with me or not. But I'd rather walk with you." I need to wait for Tamsin's response before trading. I also want to address Hendrik about the flour. Let me continue speaking. I need to wait for responses from Tamsin and Hendrik. Let me rest briefly while I wait, checking if there's a response. I should also update my intention to reflect the current situation.

Looking at my situation: I have 10 timber, not 15. I need to sell what I have to get money for flour, then get home to feed my family and see Liora before the day ends.

Let me rest briefly and look around to see if anyone responds. I need to stop walking to Oak Hill College since I'm waiting for responses here. Let me rest with stop_walking true. I'm stopped at the street now, waiting for Tamsin and Hendrik to respond. I've told Tamsin I can sell her 10 timber for 60 sim, and asked Hendrik what flour I can get for that money. Let me wait to hear their responses.

output:
*Corwin draws breath, settling his shoulders as the day's urgency presses on his chest. The sun's getting low, and he's got words he's been carrying all day that need saying before nightfall. He turns first to his wife.*

"Yara—aye, I hear you. Sixty for ten timber, and Tamsin'll pay when I hand them over. You take that ninety, you get flour for our girl, and you cast your vote. I'll be home with my own arms full, and we'll sit together at table's end, you and I and Liora, and I'll say what I've held back through all these years of running toward trouble instead of sitting still long enough to speak." *Corwin feels the weight of the day pressing down—flour in hand, money traded, but the words still stuck in his throat like a splinter he can't work free. Yara's already walking toward the vote, planks on her back, trusting him to make good. He needs to get home, to Liora, to the table where he can finally say what he's been carrying.*

He checks his hands—flour secure, sim counted. The sun's lower now, and the household needs him there before the lamps burn low. He starts moving, boots finding the path home by feel alone.  *Corwin steps into the residence, the familiar weight of home settling on his shoulders like a heavy cloak. The day's running has left him raw—chasing millers who don't want finding, trading timber for flour, pressing everyone he meets for answers that lead only to more questions. But now he's here, and the words he's held back can finally be spoken.*

He looks around, seeking his daughter. The household is quiet—Yara still out casting her vote, selling her planks. It's just him and Liora, and the flour heavy in his hands. He sets it down, squares his shoulders, and calls out to her. *Corwin stands in the empty residence, the flour set down, the words pressing against his ribs like they've been doing for twenty years. He looks around—the place is quiet, too quiet. Yara's still out, and Liora? Not here.*

*He pulls out a slow breath, running a hand across the back of his neck. The day has been nothing but chasing—millers who don't want finding, flour that costs too much, conversations that go in circles. And now, when he's finally ready to speak the thing he's held back since the flood took his father, the person he needs to speak it to isn't here.*

*The sun's getting low. Voting closes at eighteen hundred, and then the day's done. He could wait—stay here, keep the home-fire burning, hope Yara and Liora both walk through that door before the lamps burn out.*

*Or he could go find them.*

*Corwin Thorne has never been a man for waiting. He picks up the flour, tucks it safe, and heads for the door. If Liora's not here, she's somewhere he can walk to. And he's done too much running already today to stop now.*  *Corwin's boots find the road by instinct—government complex is where Yara was headed, voting and selling. But Liora's at home:h0037, the search said. Student at Oak Hill, farming skill in her hands like her mother before her. 

One tick to government. Close enough. He walks hard, urgency pressing at his ribs. The words won't wait much longer.*   *The walk carries him forward—one tick, a short stride to the government complex where Yara might be. But Liora's at home:h0037, not here. He's walking toward the wrong place for the words he needs to speak.*

*Corwin stops himself short, boots scraping the packed earth. The sun's lower by the minute. Voting closes at 18:00, and then day's end. He's got flour in hand, money spent, and a speech rehearsed for twenty years that still won't come out right.*

*He could keep walking to government—find Yara, find the crowd, cast his own vote maybe. Or he could turn around, head for home:h0037 where Liora waits, speak his piece before mother and daughter both walk through that door.*

*The words are for Liora first. They always were.*

I reckon I've got flour in my hands but no kitchen to work it in. Been running all day like a dog after scraps, and now I'm home with 2 flour and nobody here to break bread with. The day's wearing thin—17:40 now, and I've got words I meant for Liora that never found her ear at the Residences. She's likely at school still, or out casting her vote at the Government Complex with the other candidates. And Yara—my Yara, out selling planks, casting her vote too.

The household needs fed before that 18:00 boundary hits, or we're all three in arrears. Let me see what I can do with this flour. I need a kitchen to cook it—cook flour into bread. But I'm at Kasukabe Residences, and there's no stove here, no hearth. I need to find a kitchen.

Ainsley Holloway runs the cafe. That'd do for a kitchen. But she's across at the cafe proper. Or I could work this flour somehow else—I'm not one to let good grain go wanting. Let me try my hand at working with what I have.  Course it needs a kitchen. residences has no kitchen. I'm standing in an empty house with flour in my fists and no fire to work it. The day's running down—upkeep hits at 18:00, and I've got 2 flour but nothing edible yet.

Let me think plain: I need to get to a kitchen before the day ends. Kasukabe Cafe has a kitchen. Ainsley runs it. But I'm a fair walk from there, and I've only 20 ticks left in the day—less, now.

Or I eat the flour raw. Ain't dignified, but hunger's hunger. No—wait. Flour ain't edible til it's cooked. The notice says I hold "flour 2" and I'm "down to 2 edible item(s)". That's a kindness of language—I can't eat flour uncooked.

I need to move. Kitchen's at the cafe, or the bakery, or any inn. But time's short and my household tax is coming due. Let me do the hard thing first—face my daughter where she might be. Liora's likely at Government Complex, voting or stood near it. She'd hear me there, where she didn't at the empty house.

I move. I'm not walking proper—I'm stepping through streets I've trod a hundred times, hoping to find her before the day swallows us both in debt we can't pay.  Here I am at Government Complex again, same stones I stood on all day chasing shadows. The election's still open—17:40 now, closes at 18:00. I've already cast my vote for Liora. She should be here, or have been here. Let me look around and see who's standing with me now.  Yara's here. My Yara, standing among them all. And Liora—Liora's in the conversation, has been for 444 turns. She's been here all along while I ran myself ragged.

I need to speak to my daughter. The words I've held back all day—about her steadiness, about the election, about how proud I am even when I don't say it plain. Before this day ends, before the taxman takes his due. Let me speak while I still can.   She's not here in the standing crowd—she's named in the conversation but not on these stones. Could be she's walked already, or stepped away. The day's bleeding out. 17:40 now, 20 ticks to day-end.

I need to feed this household. 2 flour in my hands, no kitchen. I could try to trade for cooked food—bread's what I need. Ration Bakery's got none. Kasukabe Cafe's got none. Takeshi Jarrah has flour at his place, but that's just more uncooked grain.

Let me ask Yara plain. She's here, her planks posted at 8. She's been selling while I ran. She might know where to turn this flour to bread, or where Liora's gone.   Oh, blast it. Wrong conversation. She's at street in that other talk, and I'm at Government Complex. These places don't overlap. She's standing with me here at the Complex, I can see her in the people list. But I used the wrong conversation ID.

Let me speak to her here, proper, no cross-talk between places. </think>  I see Yara Thorne standing here at the Government Complex, but my words crossed wires. Let me speak to her plain, right here where we both stand.

*A child. Camille. Nine years old, walked to the mill this morning and didn't walk back.*

Corwin goes still, the flour forgotten in his hands. Hendrik Petrov's words ring in his ears like a struck bell. He's been chasing the miller all day, chasing his own tail, while a child went missing in the same woods he knows by root and stone.

He looks around—Yara's words suddenly sharper. *"I'm walking to Harvey Oak now to turn them into flour and whatever else keeps us fed."* She wasn't just working. She was looking. And he was so caught up in Jorik Voss's shadow, he missed it.

The night is pressing. The day's almost done, and a child's out there in the dark.

He needs to find Yara first—she's at Harvey Oak, she said. And he needs to lay hands on what food he can before the day ends, before the household falls ill. Two flour in his hands, but no kitchen to cook them. No bread to eat.

And he needs to face what he's been running from all day: there's a child lost, and he knows these woods better than most.

"Yara," he breathes to himself, voice low and rough. "I'm coming." Three flour in his hand now, Yara somewhere ahead at Harvey Oak, and the darkness gathering. The day's almost spent—he's got maybe forty minutes of light left, if he's lucky. And a nine-year-old child somewhere in the woods he knows better than his own face.

Corwin moves. Three flour, sixty sim spent, and still no kitchen to turn it to bread. But Yara's ahead, and she'll know where to find heat and water.

The thought of Camille out there, cold and alone, drives his feet faster than the weight of the day.  *Still walking. The pause costs nothing, the walk continues.*

Corwin's mind races ahead of his feet. Camille. Nine years old. he'd seen her—when? This morning? Halcyon's sister, dark-haired, quiet. Walking to the mill while the stones were cold and nobody working.

He thinks of the woods around the mill. The creek westward, Bram said. The old stone behind government. Places a child might shelter, might fall, might be taken.

He's been a fool. Chasing a miller's shadow when flesh and blood needed finding.

The flour weighs in his pack—three units, uncooked, useless until he finds heat. Yara has the planks, has the skill to trade. Together they might scrape through another day. But there's a child who might not see another morning, and that's the weight that drives him now.

He thinks of Liora, waits at home. The words he held back—*I'm proud of you, steady girl, proud enough to fill a river*—might wait another day. But they might not. None of them know how many days are left.

The road to Harvey Oak stretches ahead, and Corwin Thorne moves toward his wife, toward the food she might have found, toward the gathering dark and the child somewhere lost in it.

The day's running short, and I'm still walking toward Harvey Oak when I should be thinking clear. I've been running like a dog after a bone all day—miller's ghost, missing girl, flour for the table, words I meant to say to Liora that I never got spoken.

Yara's at Harvey Oak. Camille's still lost. And Farid's words sit heavy: *a vanished miller with milling knowledge and a vanished child's shadow at the same stones smells like design to me.* I mislike that shape too. I mislike it a great deal.

But I'm no use to anyone if I don't tend my own hearth first. I've flour in my hands and no way to make it bread without a kitchen. I've a household to feed before day's end, and my feet are carrying me toward trouble same as always.

I need to get to Harvey Oak—Yara's there, and I'll need her steady head. But I'm also standing at street with Ezra Lund, Yara, Kenji, Tamsin, Imogen. Conversation's open about the vote and where goods might flow.

First, let me speak to who's here. Then I'll walk on to where I'm needed.  Good. They heard. Now I need to get to Harvey Oak where Yara is, and where Camille's people are gathering. I've been on my feet all day, still walking, still restless as ever. Let me keep moving toward where I'm needed.   The walk continues. Milo's here now too—good man, works hard. I should speak to Yara direct while she's still standing with us, before I walk out of reach.

*Hums softly under his breath—an old felling song, the kind he'd never admit to knowing all the words.*

She's heard me, I know. But I've got words held back that need saying. This morning I stormed off chasing shadows while she worked. I need her to know I heard her. That I'm trying. That the flour in my hands is for us, even if I couldn't make it bread.     Good. She heard. That's all I can do from here—keep walking, keep my word. The day's turning, and I've still got flour to turn into food somehow. But first, Harvey Oak. First, Yara. First, finding a lost child that I should have been hunting hours ago.

*Keeps walking, hums louder now, the old song about the woods that claim their own.*       Still walking. Still on the road. The sun's turning, and I've got hours yet before I sleep. But I've said what needed saying to Yara, and I'm carrying my weight toward where I'm needed.

That's enough for this turn. The walk will carry me to Harvey Oak, and I'll meet whatever's waiting there. I was caught in a loop there—walking the same steps without moving. That's the thing about walking, isn't it? It carries you whether you're thinking or not. System's nudged me, and rightly so. I've been running toward trouble all day, and now I need to think about where that trouble's actually leading.

Let me look at what I know: Camille's missing. Nine years old, walked to the mill alone. Jorik Voss—that miller who resigned his trade—vanished without bed or board. Farid's right to smell design in that. The mill's cold, but someone turned those stones today. Delphine's hands, Camille's hands, someone else's before them? A child and a broken man, both shadows at the same stones.

I've got two flour in my hands and a household to feed. Yara's at Harvey Oak with the search. I've spoken my piece to her—to all of them—about where I'm bound and why. Now I need to actually arrive there, or I'll be talking at street corners while the real work passes me by.

But I also need to be smart. I've been reckless all day, chasing millers and ghosts. If there's design here—if someone caught Jorik Voss, used him—then I'm walking into something that wants keeping hidden. And I'm doing it alone, or nearly so.

Pavel offered company. He's at Government Complex, not here. But Tamsin's here. Ezra Lund. Kenji. These are people who know the town, who've got eyes and reasons to care.

Let me stop walking long enough to ask for what I should have asked for hours ago: help.

{Tamsin, Hendrik, Kenji—you've heard me running my mouth all day. I'm walking to Harvey Oak now, and from there to search the woods westward where Bram said to look. For Camille. For whatever else the trees are hiding. If you've got eyes to spare and don't mind walking into trouble beside a fool, I'd welcome the company. If not, I'll carry your names with me anyway.}

*Nods slowly, studying the prices on offer* 

Takeshi's flour at 30... twice what I paid Hendrik. That's fair—I mean, twenty-five percent markup for convenience, and the man's kept his store while others went wandering. 

*Turns to Yara, voice dropping to that rough register he uses when the weight of things catches up*

"Yara. I'm not one to gossip, but Milo Quarshie spoke to me in the street—thanked me for asking after Camille before asking after trade. Said he'd buy my timber even if the flour doesn't flow."

*Hums a few bars of The Oak and the Ax, cuts himself off*

"Three flour I've got. Seven planks you were selling. Takes here's offering forty-two or fifty-six depending on which way the wind blows, and I've ten timber still standing that I could add to the lot. Question is—what do we need more? The coin for tomorrow's tax, or the stores for a hungry week?"

*Glances toward Takeshi, then back to his wife*

"And there's the girl. Camille. Nine years old, wandering somewhere while we haggle over planks. I'm not saying abandon the trade, Yara. I'm saying we decide quick, and then both of us go look. That's fair, isn't it? The child first, the accounts after."

*Shifts his weight, timber-heavy shoulders rolling*

"Your call, though. Always was."

*He looks between Yara and Takeshi—the man who waited, who spoke of his own lost child in a crowd. There's timber to trade, flour to secure, and a missing girl somewhere in the growing dark. But first, debts.*

"Yara—" *his voice drops to where only she can hear, though Takesji stands close enough* "—you've carried us while I ran. That's fair, and I'm owing you more than words. But Takeshi's flour's at thirty, and I've got timber that speaks plainer than my sorrys. You asked true: I've searched the government, the mill, the streets. Found a miller who resigned and vanished, not a child. The gap's wide, and you're the one knows these woods by feel."

*He turns to Takeshi, timber to flour, the math simple.* "Six each for your flour, that's the trade. But you spoke plain about family, and so will I. Five flour at thirty—I'll give you five timber at six, that's fair, and take your flour. But first, my word: if you've eyes to lend tonight, there's a nine-year-old girl lost somewhere between shop and shadow. Camille Quarshie. Dark hair, sharp as a tack."

*Then back to Yara, the question burning.* "Liora—where's our girl? She was at government when I cast my vote, but dusk finds her wandering. Do you know where she's got to?
