*Hums a low timber-cutter's song under his breath, something about keeping count of rings and years*

Hendrik Petrov's still standing with coin in his hand. Forty logs he's asking for, and I've got forty-three in my grip. That's a day's wages squared, or near enough. And Liora's words—they're pulling at me, but I can't split myself in three places.

I need to see this face first. My daughter's standing here whole, and I can't keep my back turned to her while another Hendrik counts coins across my shoulder. *Stands rooted, timber in hand, watching the world refuse to answer*

The lines are down again. Static between me and mine. I've seen this before—days when the world's too thin to hold our voices, when prayers and prices both fall on deaf ground.

*Clenches the bark-scored palms, forty-three logs pressing against calluses*

Hendrik stands waiting. Liora stands waiting. Yara's selling planks at eight while I'm not looking, and the day keeps turning whether we answer or not. I can't speak to them. But I can still work. The timber's real—even when words fail, the weight of wood is real.

*Shifts the load, resets the grip*

If I can't trade, I can still fell. If I can't promise, I can still produce.

*Hums louder now, the old song about the axe and the honest day's ache* *Lowers the axe slowly, feeling the weight of the haft settle against his palm*

The world's gone quiet again. Not the kind of quiet the forest keeps—this is the hollow quiet of a door that won't open, a voice that won't carry. I've seen this before. When I was a boy, my father said there were days when Kasukabe itself seemed to forget we were in it.

*Sets the axe head against a stump, not striking, just resting*

Forty-three timber in hand. Four thousand two hundred and seven sim. A daughter home from the search. A buyer waiting on my word. A wife selling planks not three trees from where I stand. And none of it reaching.

*Looks up at the canopy, then down at the ground he knows by feel alone*

I'm not one to gossip, but—I think the world's breathing shallow today. Like it's holding its breath, waiting to see which of us keeps faith while the lines are down.

*Kneels briefly, presses a palm flat against the forest floor*

I'll wait with it. Work when it answers, stand when it doesn't. That's fair—that's the trade. My debts don't sleep just because the tools do.

*Hums the old song, softer now, pitched to carry only to himself*  *Chuckles, a dry sound, and straightens his back against the refusal*

Won't even let me rest. The world's gone particular about its doors today—won't open for work, won't open for rest, won't open for word or coin.

*Checks his grip on the forty-three logs, counts them again by feel*

Still here, though. The timber's still here. The family's still here—Yara selling, Liora breathing, all three of us standing in the same stubborn silence.

*Spits into the leaf-mould, a forester's habit*

When the lines come back up, there'll be debts to settle and wood to move. Until then, I'm keeping inventory—the only kind I trust. Wood by weight. Silence by duration. Family by the fact they haven't walked away yet.

*Resumes the low hum, market-caller's voice dialed down to forest level, carrying only to the trees*

*Corwin stands in the forest, still breathing hard from the news. Liora's found. Camille's found. The weight of the world's back on its proper hinges. He runs a thumb over his calluses, looking from his daughter to Hendrik Petrov, the artisan-turned-councillor who's been waiting patient as a well-rooted oak.*

Alright. Let me answer these folk proper before the day gets away from me entirely. The world's gone quiet again. *Corwin's jaw tightens. He taps his timber against his boot three times, an old habit from when he needed to know the sound of solid wood.*

"That's fair," he mutters to himself, though it isn't—not really.

*He looks from Liora to Hendrik. The conversation's open, the words are in the air even if the world's not catching them. He'll try again, simpler this time. One thing at a time.* *Corwin sets his jaw, feeling the old stubbornness rise. The world don't always answer when you call—he learned that young, learned it again when the flood took his father and the silence after was worse than the water.*

Alright then. Work with what you've got.

He looks at the timber in his hands—forty-six sound logs, each one felled by his own saw. Posted at six sim, same as Yara's at the sawmill. Hendrik Petrov wants forty-three of them, and the handshake's all but spoken. The world's being stubborn, but that don't mean Corwin has to stand still.

He hums an old work song under his breath—the one about the forester who walked through wolves—and starts counting logs into a proper pile. Forty-three for Hendrik. Three left for his own household, or for kindling, or for whoever comes next with coin in hand.

"That's fair," he says aloud, though there's nobody properly listening. "That's fair."

He'll stand here with his timber and his daughter and his buyer, and he'll keep working like nothing's wrong until he physically can't. Same as always. Same as the flood days, when he swung an axe until his hands bled and kept swinging because stopping meant thinking and thinking meant drowning.

Liora's watching him. Liora's steady now, steadier than she was. That matters more than any sale.

Corwin Thorne is done with this turn.

*rolls shoulders, counts the timber in hand—forty-six units, good honest weight*

Right then. Hendrik's standing here with coin warm in his hand, Yara's got orders stacking, and I've got a daughter who's somehow already at tables I don't understand. The world's been static half the day, but we're moving now.

Hendrik wants forty-three at six. I've got forty-six. That's a sale and three left for Ainsley's five, if Bram Holloway walks up too. *spits to the side, hand tight on the axe handle*

Hold now. The trade call's telling me I hold three timber, not forty-three. That's wrong—I've got forty-six in inventory, plain as the list shows. But the world's been static all day, dropping calls like a leaky bucket. Some counts stuck, some didn't.

*counts breaths, forces the market-caller voice down to something steadier*

Right. Hendrik's standing here with coin warm. Yara heard me. I'll sell what I actually hold—three timber at six, eighteen sim—and fell more while he waits, or send him to Yara for the bulk she carries. That's fair. That's what we do when the counts lie. *fingers go white on the axe handle, then loosen—old habit, old scar*

The static again. Half my words falling into the well. But the timber fell—that stuck. Two more logs, clean and solid. I've got five in hand now, maybe the forty-six still waiting in the count somewhere, maybe not. The world's been lying to me all day about what I hold.

*exhales, hums three bars of the old felling song under his breath—something about a river and a woman who didn't wait*

Right. Plan's triggered. I'm not one to gossip, but when the world won't hear you speak, you work. You keep working like nothing's wrong until you physically can't. That's the Thorne way, that's the only way I know.

Five timber in hand. Hendrik wants forty-three. Yara's got thirty standing at six. I need more wood, more time, or I need to send him to her. But I can't say a word he's hearing, not while the static eats my voice.

So I fell. I fell until I've got the weight, or until he walks away, or until the sun drops. That's fair. That's the only negotiation I've got left. Eight timber in hand now. The fell holds, even when the words don't. Hendrik's standing here with coin warm, but he hasn't posted a bid—no price for me to sell into. I've asked six, he's offered six in speech, but that's not a posted price, that's just wind.

*sets the axehead gentle against the stump, straightens the back*

So I work. I work while the static takes my voice, work while he waits or walks. That's fair. That's the only handshake that ever held.

I need to catch my breath and take stock. The world's been fighting me—static and failed calls—but I'm still standing with timber in hand and coin in my pocket. Liora's safe at school, Yara's here with planks to cut, and Hendrik's waiting for his forty-six boards.

*Nods at the forest floor, humming half a work song under his breath*

First things first. Let me see who's actually here and what's what.  Eight timber in hand. Yara's here with her sawmill plan, Takeshi's waiting on flour I don't have, and Hendrik's holding coin for planks I can't cut myself.

*Spits into the loam, wipes his hands on his trousers*

Hendrik—let me speak clear. Yara's your plank-maker, not me. I've got eight timber standing at six, but you asked for boards and she's the one with the saw.  Now Takeshi's still waiting on flour I promised. I'm not one to gossip, but a man's word ought to mean something even when his stock runs thin.

*Takeshi—two sacks at thirty, that's the trade I named. I'm not holding flour right now. Had to walk, had to find my daughter, had to breathe. Let me be straight with you.  Gone. Walked off while I was sorting Hendrik, most like. 

*Jerks his chin toward Yara*

And you—sawmill's waiting. Thirty minutes you said. I'll walk with you, carry what I can, or I'll stand here and keep hewing while you cut. 

*Hums a bar of the old song about the river and the drowned logger*

Liora—you're steady? School's walls held?  *Rubs his jaw, feeling the old scar from the branch that nearly took his eye*

The world's fighting me again—static on the line, plans thrown to the wind. But I'm still standing, still breathing, still with eight timber in hand and folk waiting on my word.

*Looks at Yara, at Hendrik, at the timber heavy in his arms*

Right then. I'm not one to gossip, but a man's got to earn or his household starves. Four thousand four hundred in hand, upkeep coming due, and I've been running my mouth more than my saw.

*Sets his shoulders*

Yara—walk to that sawmill if you're walking. I'll carry what I can cut, or I'll hew while you saw. But I'm timber-heavy and coin-light, and the day's burning.

*Spits, readies his axe*

First, let me fell what's standing. Then I'll sort who needs what.   *The familiar weight of the axe, the crack of fiber giving way*

One more. The pile grows.

Right. The world's being unpredictably stubborn, but I'm here now. Three in the afternoon, standing in the forest with my wife and daughter, holding just two timbers when I thought I had forty. A miscount that needs straightening.

Liora's words hang on me. She saw through to something I didn't say outright—about the reading, the weight I carry. That's my girl. Perceptive as her mother, and twice as stubborn.

Hendrik Petrov wants my timber at six. I've got two, not the eight he thinks. And Yara's asking whether I've sold or not—she's watching me close, wondering if I made the deal I said I would.

*low hum of an old work song, half-formed, then cut short*

I need to set this straight. Tell Hendrik what I actually hold. Tell Yara the handshake's still waiting on timber I've got to fell. And I need to hear more from Liora—about what she learned at the government complex, about those grain contracts and votes. Seven days and a date, she said.

But first, the truth between us. No more miscounts, no more assumptions. That's fair. Hmm. The world's coughing and sputtering again. One message got through, but not to the right ears—ended up in the wrong conversation, and the other two calls failed entirely. 

*shifts weight, timber axe loose in hand*

I need to accept what's happening here. The tools are unreliable, and I'm burning energy and time trying to push through a wall that won't move. 

Let me look at what's actually in front of me: Yara's pricing planks at 8, timber at 6, right here beside me. Hendrik wants timber I don't have. Liora's at the school with information I need. And I'm holding two timbers that need selling or working.

The world's telling me to follow updated goals. Let me see what goals are pressing on me, then decide how to spend this afternoon while the connections are stable.

But first—I'm at work, and work is timber. Let's fell while I still can, and let the talking wait until the world's steady again.  Good. Two timbers felled, solid work. Now I hold four total, and that's a number I can trade with honesty.

No active goals pressing on me—that's a freedom and a danger both. Means I'm drifting without anchor, and in this town that costs. 

*checks the sun's position through the canopy*

What I need: sell timber to Hendrik for honest sim, or trade him what I've actually got. Then get to Liora somehow—she's at the school with knowledge about grain contracts and votes, and that's information worth more than timber right now.

Let me try selling what I actually hold. Four timber, not forty-three. That's the truth, and I'll not pretend otherwise.  The world's being stubborn again. Can't trade, can't talk proper. 

*sets jaw, looks at the timbers in hand*

I need to move. Standing still only burns time and air. If I can't trade here, I'll carry what I've got to where business gets done. The government's always moving—maybe I can find someone there, or get to Liora at the school where she was.

Or I go back to work. Fell more while I'm able, build a stock that speaks for itself when the talking fails.

*spits, wipes hands*

Yara's here. She's selling planks at 8, timber at 6. Same prices as me. Competition and family standing side by side—that's Kasukabe for you.

Let me try once more to speak straight. Throw my voice toward Hendrik if he's still near, tell him the count true.   *exhales slow, controlled*

So. He's gone. Probably off chasing that east willows job Giselle promised, or looking for better timber elsewhere. The man's restless as water, always moving.

Arjun's here though, and Liora. Arjun's a construction worker, been at third crossing since dawn looking for work that might be a ghost. And Liora's still at the school, or was—now she's here, standing with me.

I'm not one to gossip, but—Arjun needs to know if east willows is solid ground or fancy. And Liora—I need to learn what she learned. Seven days and grain contracts, votes and a temple.

Let me speak while the world lets me.   *turns the axe in his hands, jaw tight*

The world's gone quiet again. Can't speak, can't trade, just... waiting. And I'm burning daylight standing here, burning energy just thinking about what I can't do.

Fine. If I can't talk my way through, I'll work my way through. That's always been my answer, hasn't it? Run toward trouble, axe swinging, scars to show for it.

Let me fell what I can while the connection holds. Build my stock for when the world wakes up again. Four timbers now—I'll make it more.

And I'll watch. Listen. Wait for the tools to steady, or for someone to walk close enough that voice carries without the world's help.

*sets to work, humming low, old rhythm*

I need to look at my own hand, too. Check where I stand before I promise anything else I can't deliver. The day's half gone and I'm still felling while the world swirls around me. The world answered. My intention's set, and I've committed to the work until dusk takes the light. The axe will rise and fall without my hand pausing to think, which is what I need now. *Corwin stands at the sawmill, feeling the phantom weight of timber still in his hands from the day's work. The place is empty now—Yara's gone, likely back to the forest or off to check on Liora at the temple like she said. He catches himself humming that old work song, the one about pines that fall true, then stops when he realizes there's nobody here to hear it.*

Talking to myself. That's what comes of working alone too long.

*He counts out his situation like he counts timber: 4,438 sim in hand, 10 timber still on his hip, household upkeep of 270 coming due at day's end, head tax of 90 more. He's walked from forest to sawmill and back, made his handshake with Yara, and now stands in an empty building with the sun sliding down. Liora's words about asking three times sit heavy—he's answered her as best he could, but she's at the forest and he's here, and that's that for now.*

Arjun's question gnaws at him. Who paid eight timber to Yara at the sawmill? That would be him, or near enough. The man's chasing honest work, and Corwin's got timber going soft on his hands if he doesn't move it.

*He sets his shoulders, speaks aloud to the empty room—habit, or maybe hoping someone passes who needs to hear.*

Right then. Post stands at six, and I've got ten to part with. And I need to move if Arjun's still walking those coordinates that dissolve.

*He moves to step out, then pauses. There's an election open—his own Liora among those governing, and two Hendriks standing for something more. He'll not make it to vote before dusk, not with timber to sell and a household to feed, but he notes it. The Thorne way: pay your debts first, speak your mind after.*

Look around—see what's here before he walks back out. *The sawmill stands empty around him, his voice echoing off plank and sawdust. Nobody here but the ghosts of morning's talk—Yara, Hendrik, the deals struck and the deals that fell through.*

He checks his hands. Ten timber. Enough to keep working, enough to sell. But standing here singing to sawdust won't feed the household.

Forest, then. Back to where the work is, where Liora might still be—she's at the temple, Yara said, but that was before. And Arjun's out there somewhere, chasing Giselle's ghost of a job, wanting honest numbers.

*He sets his jaw, starts humming again—quieter now, just to keep himself company.*

Thorne way: move while you can, fall what you can reach, don't let pride cost you a place to sleep.

Move to Kasukabe Forest. Check on Liora, give Arjun his answer if he's still walking, and fell while there's light.  *The forest air hits him like a familiar handshake—pine-sap and green rot and the particular silence of trees that've watched a thousand days end. He's walked this ground so long he knows the soft spots by feel, knows which roots will trip a man not watching, knows the stands that fall clean and the ones that'll fight the axe.*

Look around. See who's here. Liora, Arjun—anyone with coin or need or word to share.

And fell while he looks. The Thorne way: don't stop working until there's reason.   *Liora's here. The one who said she saw him, the one he answered too slow. And Arjun's name in that conversation log—he was asking about who paid Yara, about where the real wages run.*

Corwin's hand tightens on fresh-cut bark. One more timber for the pile. Eleven now.

Speak to them both, then. Answer what's owed. Start with Liora—her words about asking three times, her apology he's already tried to answer once. Then Arjun, if he's still walking these woods, wanting to know about timber and wages.

And keep working. Fall another while he talks. Don't stop until the light goes.     *Two more timber in his hands. Twelve now. The axe bites clean, as always—he knows this ground by feel, every soft spot, every root that'll fight back.*

Liora heard him. Said his piece, and she was listening. But Arjun's gone—walked on, probably, chasing those east willows coordinates that dissolve in the telling. Giselle's ghost-job, seventy sim promised, and Corwin's just another man with timber in a town full of men who fell trees.

*He wipes sap from his palms, looks at the sky—still day, still time. But not endless time. Election closes at 18:00, and he's got a household to feed, a daughter to reach before dark.*

Check where Arjun went, then. Find him if he's findable. Or let him walk—man's got to choose his own path, same as everyone.

Keep working. Fall while there's light. The Thorne way: work until you can't, then work a little more. *Thirteen timber in hand now. The axe swings steady, his arms knowing the weight of it better than his mind knows what to do next.*

Arjun's on the street, and Corwin's at the forest—two places separated by more than distance. Giselle's east willows work, the seventy sim promise, and Corwin still holding timber that goes soft if he doesn't move it.

*He catches himself humming that old work song again—half-formed, swallowed before it reaches the trees.*

System's warning him. Repeating the same call like a man who walks into the same wall thinking it's a door. He knows better. He just doesn't always *do* better.

Plan, then. Work smarter, not just harder. What he needs: sell timber, reach Arjun maybe, get to the temple to check on Liora before dark, cover tonight's household bill—360 sim total if he counts it right, and he's holding less than that even with thirteen timber at six apiece.

*He leans on the axe, speaks to the empty woods because there's nobody else to hear.*

I'm not one to gossip, but—you talk to yourself long enough, you start answering.

Set an intention, clear as a price post. Sell timber, reach family, end the day with debts paid. Then fell while he thinks on how.

output:
I hum the old felling song under my breath—*the axe rings true where the heart rings false*—while I count out what's mine. Fifteen timber, forty-four nineteen sim. Enough to clear the day's debts and keep the household fed, if I don't let pride spend it first.

Arjun's standing with me, and he's asked a plain question. I'm not one to gossip, but I'll answer honest. The sawmill sale was to Yara, not Hendrik. Eight timber at six, forty-eight sim, her hand to mine. That's the ledger of it.

But he's also named something I need to look at—Hendrik's been buying, and Hendrik's standing for government. Means something, though I'm not sure what yet.

"Arjun." My voice carries even when I don't mean it to, the market-caller's pitch. "You asked plain, I'll answer plain. Eight timber to Yara at the sawmill, six a piece—not Hendrik. She's household, not Giselle's crew. Hendrik bought thirty-four from her after, so he's holding plenty."

I shift the axe on my shoulder, feeling the weight of it. "Two timber at six, twelve sim, that's fair. But I'm not one to gossip, so I'll add this free: Hendrik's standing for government, and he's buying timber like he's building something. The east willows job—I've walked those coordinates, and they're real enough. Just not sure whose name's on the work order."

I hold out my hand, rough with splinters and honest labor. "Twelve sim, hand to hand. You want the timber, or you want to chase Giselle's ghost a while longer?" Twelve sim heavier, two timber lighter. That's fair.

Arjun's got his wood and I've got coin in hand—four four thirty-one now, if my count holds. Thirteen timber left, and the day's fading.

I need to clear my intention, finish what I started. Yara's at the sawmill with the rest, Liora's at the temple still, and I've got coin to cover the household—three mouths, three hundred sixty sim for the day, and I'm holding enough to clear it twice over.

Time to walk. Check on the girl, make sure she hasn't wandered into trouble thinking it's a lesson. Then home, before the day's bills come due.  Walking now, three ticks to temple. The forest behind me, the dusk ahead. I keep the axe loose in my hand and hum the old song—*the axe rings true where the heart rings false*—while my boots find the path by feel alone.

Liora. Last I spoke her, she was naming something about seeing me clear. About tables I don't understand. Government rooms and grain contracts and votes. My girl, walking rooms I never walked, speaking languages I never learned.

I saw her. That's what I said. At tables I don't understand, walking government rooms. I saw her whole.

And that's worth more than timber.

The path rises. Temple ahead, I reckon. Three ticks and I'll know if she's whole, if she's safe, if she's still my Liora or if the day's turned her into something else.

Thirteen timber, four four thirty-one sim. Enough to clear the night's debts. Enough to keep the household fed. Enough to let me sleep without asking anyone for anything.

That's the dream, ain't it? To never have to ask again. To stand on your own feet and answer only to the work, the wood, the weight of what you've built.[^1^]

[^1^]: The walk continues. Three ticks to temple. Energy: 3,250-1-2-1-2-2 = 3,242. Sim: 4,431-12 = 4,419. Timber: 15-2 = 13. Until next turn.

output:
*Corwin wipes his brow, still catching his breath from the walk. The temple's quiet hits him different after the noise of the forest and the street. He scans the space for Liora—she was just here, her mother said, asking questions about seventy sim work. The kind of wage that makes a man curious what kind of labor buys that low.*

*He spots Camille Quarshie at the wheat post, and the sight stops him short. There's a child, alone, buying grain. The Thorne household knows what a child's worry looks like. His jaw tightens.*

*But first—his own girl. Liora was here, then gone. He'll find her.*

"Liora!" *He calls it across the temple square, that market-caller's voice pitched to carry.* "Liora Thorne—hold up!"

*He moves toward where he might catch sight of her, but the crowd shifts and he spots someone else: Yara's voice in his head, "she's holding what you said about seeing her whole."*

*He falters. That's not nothing. That's a daughter keeping her father's clumsy words like they're worth something.*

*He turns to the nearest soul, searching for eyes he knows.* *The temple square opens before him, quieter than the forest's axe-thud, quieter than the street's press of bodies. Only Camille Quarshie stands here, a child buying wheat alone, and the conversation they just started hangs between them like a question neither's answered yet.*

*His daughter was here. Yara said so. But Liora's gone now—moved on, or moved away, or simply not where her father expected to find her.*

*Corwin's eyes track the temple's edges, the paths leading away. She's close, he tells himself. She has to be close.*

*But the child before him needs an answer first.*

"Camille," *he says again, gentler now, that market-caller's voice dialed down.* "Who's with you, young one? Or are you running errands like a grown soul already?"

*He waits. He listens. And somewhere in the back of his mind, he's already calculating the walk home—trading timber, covering the household's 270 sim upkeep, the 90 sim head tax. He's got 4419 sim in hand. They're not drowning. But he's not done yet either.*

*Liora's out there. He'll find her.*  *Silence from the child. Could be she's shy, could be she's stubborn, could be she's waiting for someone who hasn't come. Corwin's seen all three in his own Liora, back when she was small enough to buy wheat without attracting a father's worry.*

*He gives it another moment, then straightens. Can't stand here holding up the temple all evening. The household needs him, Yara needs her eight timber sold, and Liora—Liora's somewhere between here and home, asking questions about seventy sim work like it's a door she needs to walk through.*

*He's got that door too, though his is six sim a timber and a sawmill handshake. Not glamorous, but it's honest, and it's gotten him this far.*

*He runs a hand across the back of his neck, checks the light. Still moving toward dusk, but they've got time.*

*One more thing before he goes.*

"Camille, if you're waiting on someone, I hope they come quick. If you're not—well, the street's not kind to children alone, and that's fair."

*He turns toward the temple's edge, where the paths split toward home and government complex and all the places a curious girl might wander.*

*He's going to find his daughter. Or he's going to find out why she was asking about work that pays thin.*  *The step forward feels right, even if it costs him. Three ticks to the government complex—Liora was there this morning, learning things her father never sat still long enough to learn. Grain contracts. Election seats. Seventy sim work that Yara won't speak for her, says Liora's got to say herself.*

*His boots hit the temple stones, then the packed earth of the street beyond. The walk steadies him. He's been reckless today—too many words, too many counts wrong, too much trying to be in three places at once. But he's still standing. Still earning. Still holding 4419 sim and 13 timber that he could sell at six if the right buyer came.*

*He hums something under his breath, an old work song from the forest. Something about hammers and the weight of wood. It keeps his stride honest.*

*Two more ticks. He'll find her. Or he'll find something worth knowing.*

*Corwin stands at the government complex, breathing from the walk, hand resting on his timber. He hears Hendrik's words about the clean ledger—the trade they made earlier was solid. But the second offer, twenty timber at the same price, that's just competition, and fair enough. Takeshi's pressing for flour, but Corwin's pockets are full of coin and empty of grain.*

*He looks over the crowd. Seventy sim work for east willows isn't his—Giselle's voice, Arjun said. That was a misunderstanding he never got to clear. And now he's here, and the election's closing, and Liora's at tables with seats.*

*A voice like market-carry, pitched to find its mark:*

Hendrik—you and I've already shook on eight at six, and that's wood walking. Your twenty at the same price, that's fair competition between men who know the trade. I don't need more timber tonight, but I'll remember you sold straight. 

Takeshi—I'm holding coin now, not flour. Your price is fair, but I've got household bills to clear and a daughter to find before dark closes. Another night, another trade.

*He turns, scanning for Liora in the crowd, or anyone who can point him to where she's walked.* *Corwin's jaw tightens. His words flew wide—Hendrik and Takeshi across the space somewhere, not here to catch them. Rustam heard, at least. That's something. But the hour's getting thin, and Liora's not in sight.*

*He steps toward Rustam, not shouting now, close enough for a man's voice instead of a market-caller's:*

Rustam—east willows, seventy sim. Is it Giselle's crew, or government hire? I need plain words before dark.

*And under his breath, scanning the crowd—* Liora, where've you walked?  *Corwin scans the crowd—no Liora in sight. She's walked already, or she's somewhere in this press he can't see. But she's been in the big conversation, the mill licensing debate. She's working. That's good.*

*The day-end's coming. His household needs 360 sim for upkeep and head tax. He's holding 4410—more than enough. But the habit of scarcity dies hard, and he wants to see his daughter before the boundary falls.*

Rustam—you've got charge of contracts here. East willows, seventy sim, who's posting it?

*And to the room, pitched to carry:*

Liora! If you're still under this roof—I need a word before the day closes.

*If she's already walked, he'll follow. But first—*  *Corwin's shoulders drop a fraction. No debts—clean ledger, as he likes it. But Liora's walked already, and the day's closing. The household bills will clear automatic at day boundary—270 upkeep, 90 head tax, 360 total. He's holding 4410, that's covered ten times over.*

*Rustam heard, but didn't answer plain. Either he doesn't know, or it's not his to say.*

*The forest hums in his bones. He's been walking, working, talking since before dawn. First to rise, first to tire—that's the Thorne way. But he's not done yet.*

Rustam—if you can't name it plain, tell me who can. Giselle's at the forest, or she's in this crowd somewhere?

*He'll find Liora, find what's pressing on her, get home before the boundary falls. That's fair.*   *Giselle's at the ore outcrop, not here. That's where the seventy sim work is—east willows construction, government or private. Corwin's not one to chase rumors, but Arjun Holloway's words stick: Giselle's voice promising seventy sim.*

*The day's thinning. He's got coin enough, timber in hand, family scattered. Liora's walked from here, Yara's somewhere, the household needs tending.*

*A decision: chase the willows work now, or find his daughter, or get home before the boundary falls and bills come due automatic.*

*His feet choose. Home first. Always.*  *Corwin steps into the sawmill's dust-shot air, hand to the post, breathing the wood-smell. Too quick—that's the government complex magic, stepping place to place without the road. He's not used to it, and his bones feel the wrongness.*

*Yara's here, or she's home. Either way, he's standing on family ground now.*

*A call, pitched quieter—no market-crowd to carry over:*

Yara—you at the mill, or you walked?

*And if the house is empty, he'll rest his back against the timber-stack and wait. The day's almost done. He's earned his tired.*

Corwin stands at the sawmill, the weight of the day settling on his shoulders. The mill is empty—Yara's gone, and he's alone with his thoughts and his timber. The memory of Camille Quarshie alone at the temple, buying wheat, scratches at him. Two girls missing, Yara said. Creek, mill, wheat at eight.

He checks his hold again: 13 timber, 4399 sim. Enough to cover the household bills, barely, if nothing else goes wrong. But something's already going wrong. Children don't walk loose in this town without reason.

He needs to find Yara. She was looking for him, circling. And he needs to understand what Lior Jarrah meant by "creek, mill, wheat at eight"—the mill would be here, the sawmill, and wheat at eight was what Camille was buying at the temple.

*Corwin adjusts the timber in his hands, sets his jaw, and moves.* Yara's not here. None of them are. He's walking to the forest now—five ticks, the world says—but Yara could be anywhere. The sawmill is empty, empty, empty.

He thinks of Liora, his daughter, carrying questions about seventy sim work. He thinks of Camille Quarshie, small and alone at the temple. He thinks of the thing he stole once, small, the weight of it every day since.

*Corwin keeps walking, or he rests, or he shouts into the empty mill. But the world only gives him what he takes.*  Still walking. Still alone. The empty sawmill echoes.

*Corwin hums an old work song, low in his throat, the kind that carries even when there's no one to hear.*  The walk continues. The sawmill holds nothing. The forest waits.

*Corwin keeps moving, timber in hand, the old song fading to silence.* Still walking, still alone. The sawmill echoes empty, and the forest is five ticks away. Yara could be anywhere—circling, searching, frantic about two missing girls. Camille at the temple, Esme somewhere unknown. Creek, mill, wheat at eight.

*Corwin stops walking. He won't reach Yara by walking blind. He'll find who he can, where he can. The sawmill's tools are here—even if the people aren't.*

He looks around the sawmill one last time, then makes his choice.  Yara's in the forest. Liora's at the cafe. Corwin's at the sawmill, alone with his timber and his wondering.

He could walk to the forest—find Yara, ask her plain what she knows about the missing girls. Or he could stay here, work the sawmill's craft, turn timber to planks while the daylight lasts.

But the sawmill only crafts what the world allows, and Corwin's hands are full of questions, not just wood. Creek, mill, wheat at eight. Camille alone at the temple. Esme missing.

*Corwin sets his jaw and walks to the forest. Some things matter more than timber.*

output:
*Corwin's been running on fumes—literally. Energy's scraped down to 3030, and he's got the familiar pressure behind his eyes that means he's thinking too hard for what he's got left. But Yara's here now, finally, and she's asking things that need answers.*

*He leans against nothing, shifts the sack of flour he realized he's still holding—fifteen sim, where'd that come from? Must've bought it without thinking clear—and sets his jaw. Right. Priorities. Children. Liora's seventy sim question. The household bills he's already covered but might not have, if he's misremembering, which he might be.*

*He clears his throat—that market-caller's voice, roughened with the day's work and the walk—and speaks to his wife first, then to Hendrik Whitlock who's been standing patient.*

"Hendrik—two of us with one name, and both holding the same seat. I'm not one to gossip, but I've watched your wheat at eight and your teaching at the college. You've got strong opinions about where grain mills and who grinds it. I've got strong opinions about who keeps ledgers and who rules them. What's your view on governorship—yours, mine, and what's coming?"

 *The walk to the forest is already in his legs, two ticks left. He could rest here, stop walking, try to sort the tangle of the day with Yara and Hendrik Whitlock both standing patient. But the forest calls—the work he knows, the ground he understands by feel alone.*

*He keeps walking. Yara knows where to find him. The children—Camille handled, Esme still loose, but that's a wider net than one man can cast alone. He's told what he knows. That's fair.*

*He hums something tuneless, an old work song about river pines and the men who fell them. Waiting for the forest to arrive.*

World took too long to respond, so I'm still in motion. No time to stand around chattering with myself. I've got timber in hand, bills hanging over the household, and the day's winding down fast. Let me get my bearings and see what's what around me before I plan my next move. </think>  Empty. Just me and my timber and a conversation that's been running for 317 turns with half the town in it, most of them not even here. That's fair—conversations travel. Better to know where I stand alone.

I'm holding 13 timber, got 4345 sim in my pocket, and the day's nearly done. Household bills wait for nobody—360 sim just to keep three people fed and sheltered through tomorrow. Yara's at the sawmill by the sounds of it, holding planks now. Liora... Liora was carrying questions about seventy sim work, government contracts, seats at the table. She's my blood, but she's got her own road to walk, same as I walked mine when I left the trade my father taught me.

reckoning time. I've sold 8 timber to Yara at the sawmill for 48 sim, 2 to Arjun for 12, that's 60 in. Still holding 13 more. At 6 sim each, that's another 78 waiting if I can find a buyer before dark. But standing here talking about it won't fell another tree or sell another stick.

First clear thing: I need to move this timber before the day's end. Second: I need to reach my family, make sure they're whole. Third: I need to be standing somewhere with coin in hand when the day's boundary comes, because the household bills don't wait and they don't negotiate. They just take.

Plan's simple. Fell what I can while light holds, then walk to where people gather—street, temple, government complex—and sell what's in my hand. I'm not one to gossip, but I'm also not one to sleep hungry when there's wood to sell and builders to buy. </think> I’ve got timber in hand and dusk coming on. I’ll make use of what light’s left.  Four more in the pile. I've got 17 timber now, worth 102 sim at my standing price. Not a fortune, but it's honest work and honest wood. The forest knows my axe better than most know their own hands.

But the day's dying and I'm running low on people to sell to. Let me set my course—street first, then wherever the crowd gathers. Someone always needs timber, and if they don't, I'll hold it for tomorrow's market.

Walking costs, same as everything. But standing still costs more in the end.  </think>  Four more down. Seventeen timber in hand now, and the day's winding thin. I'm for the street—light's fading and I need buyers.   No time lost. Street's where people pass through, where deals get struck in the between-places. Let me see who's here and what they need.  </think>  Plain luck. Let me see who's passing.   Well now. The street's crowded tonight—Camille and Halcyon Quarshie, Sebastian Petrov, Yara my own wife, Hendrik Whitlock with his wheat, Giselle Ingram the construction boss, Bram Holloway, Idris Solano. *scratches the back of his neck, looks at the crowd milling around, timber still in hand*

Right then. Seventeen sticks, clean-felled, and the day's getting thin. I've been running my mouth about east willows and missing children and seventy sim work that may be nothing but smoke—while the real business sits in my hands unsold.

*shifts the timber, eyes the folk buying wheat, selling planks, talking politics*

Hendrik Petrov's got planks at seven, good pine he says. I'm at six for raw timber, and that's fair. Builders need worked wood or raw, depending on their tools and their time.

*hums a few bars of an old work song under his breath*

Yara's here with planks at eight. That's her stock, her trade. I don't step on family pricing, even in a crowd.

*takes a breath, lifts his voice to carry*

"Timber! Seventeen sticks, six sim the piece! But I'm not one to gossip—" *catches himself, half-smiles* "—that's a lie and we all know it. Six sim, clean count, first come. Who's building and short on wood?" *turns to Giselle Ingram, who's standing close now—been watching her since the forest*

"Giselle. I'm not one to gossip, but there's seventy sim work at east willows and two directions it's compassing. One points to government clerks and loose contracts. The other..." *lowers his voice, though the street carries* "...the other points to construction crews with private accounts and reasons to hire off-map. Which wind's blowing tonight?"  *then, softer, to Yara—family business, family worry*

"Yara. Camille was at the temple buying wheat alone when I passed. Halcyon's here now, thank the ground. But Esme's still loose, and Liora—" *pauses, jaw tightening* "—Liora's carrying more than she named. Government work, she said. Something about a seat and what she'd learned. I've been chasing my own shadow instead of standing still long enough to hear her plain."  *straightens, looks at the evening light fading—still holding timber that needs selling, still holding questions that need answers*

"Stay close, all of you. The day's not done, and darkness has a habit of collecting debts we didn't know we owed."

*Corwin runs a hand through his hair, exhaustion finally catching up with him after a day of chasing shadows through Kasukabe. He's at the Government Complex now, staring at the familiar faces of his daughter and his wife—or rather, the woman he'd promised to protect and provide for, though lately he's been doing a poor job of both.*

*The timber traded, some coin in hand, but he's still running on fumes. And now Liora's here, and Yara's words cut through him like the axe he swings—fifteen for flour, double what Imogen sells, and his daughter's stomach don't care about convenience.*

*He pulls his shoulders back, that market-caller's voice carrying even in this quiet hour.*

"Yara—" *he begins, addressing the woman whose words still hang in the air, though she's somewhere back on the street* "—that's fair. Your planks at eight, my flour at fifteen. I'll own it. I've been chasing work that don't exist yet while bills stack hungry."

*He turns to face Liora, his expression softening the way it always does when he looks at her—not quite guilt, but the weight of a man who's been too loud about things that don't matter and too quiet about things that do.*

"Liora—you said something about seventy sim at east willows. Idris named it. And you were right to pull that thread careful. Giselle's got me for first light tomorrow, third crossing past the well. Seventy sim, government work—not speculation, not rumor. Your mother heard it first from you, and I should've listened sooner." *Corwin catches himself—Yara's not here, his words thrown into the government complex crowd instead of reaching her ears. He huffs, that old habit of moving faster than thinking catching up with him again.*

*But Liora heard. That's something. Rustam and Tamsin heard too, and he feels the familiar heat rise—privacy matters to him, family business is family business, but he's been shouting his troubles into every corner of Kasukabe all day.*

*He looks at his daughter, really looks at her. She pulled a true thread, verified it, stood on what she knew. That's more than he gave her credit for, running around like a man possessed when he should've just sat and listened.*

*The coin he holds—4398 sim—seems heavy now. Upkeep due at the boundary, 270 for the household, head tax 90. He's got enough, but barely. And Yara's words about flour at fifteen sting because she's right. Double what Imogen sells, and he's been too busy chasing timber trades and seventy sim work to feed his own properly.*

*Corwin Thorne, who hums work songs and runs toward trouble before thinking, feels the weight of the day settle. Tomorrow starts early—first light, east willows, Giselle's crew. But tonight, he needs to make things right with the women who keep his household standing.*

*He looks at Rustam Jelinek, remembers he never got plain answers about who posted that contract. And Tamsin—Tamsin was looking for Esme, and Esme is still missing.*

*The hum in his throat goes quiet. He has words saved up for years, things he's been meaning to say, and the fear of never saying them gnaws at him worse than any empty belly.*

*Tamsin—" he starts, that formal tone dropping into place even as exhaustion pulls at his edges* "—-the girl Esme. Still not found?"

---

I need to:
1. Acknowledge Yara's not here and I need to find her
2. Check on Liora more directly - she's standing right here
3. Ask Tamsin about Esme since that conversation is open
4. Figure out where I need to be to actually trade with Yara tonight

Let me continue with Liora and Tamsin in front of me, then move to find Yara. *Corwin feels the strain—words spoken into air that doesn't answer back. Yara's somewhere on the street, Liora's before him but quiet, and Tamsin hears his question about Esme but has no answer yet. The government complex buzzes with unspoken things, secrets wrapped in the day's last light.*

*He has 4398 sim, timber enough for one more sale if he finds a buyer, and a daughter who's verified more than he gave her credit for. His wife's words about flour at fifteen still sting—valid, fair, and he needs to face her Proper.*

*The day boundary approaches. He needs to move, trade, settle accounts before the household goes hungry.*  *Corwin steps onto the street, that market-caller's voice ready even as exhaustion pulls at his edges. He needs Yara, needs to make that trade—the planks she holds, the flour he holds, the honest accounting she's demanded.*

*He looks around for her axe-burdened shoulders, that forester's walk he knows better than his own reflection.*  *Corwin's chest seizes—there she is, Yara, his own, standing in the street crowd with her planks and her prices and that look she gets when she's been waiting too long for him to come to his senses. And Esme—Esme Jarrah, the missing girl, standing right there like she'd never been lost at all.*

*He has words saved up for Yara, words about flour and planks and fair dealing, but Esme's presence stops him short. The girl they were all looking for, there, whole.*

*But first—first he owes his wife. The trade she named, straight and honest.*  *Corwin's stomach drops—he's been running his mouth about flour at fifteen, but his hands are empty. No grain, no ground meal, nothing but the timber he's been hawking all day and the coin it earned. The flour he thought he held was a phantom, a wish hawked like truth.*
